bull_thesis:
CECONOMY is the parent of MediaMarkt and Saturn, Europe's largest consumer-electronics retail network across eleven countries, and the bullish case is that a genuine operating turnaround is being priced as though it were not happening. The improvement is visible in filed, unadjusted numbers rather than only in management's preferred measure: revenue in the third quarter to 30 June 2026 rose 9.8% year on year to EUR 5.27 billion, and the reported operating loss in what is structurally the weakest quarter of the retail year halved from minus EUR 82 million to minus EUR 44 million. Full-year 2024/25 revenue reached EUR 23.07 billion and free cash flow rose 180% to EUR 337 million. Trailing twelve-month free cash flow through June 2026 is EUR 731 million against an equity value of roughly EUR 1.9 billion.

The structural argument is the mix. Management has moved the share of gross profit coming from higher-margin activities outside the traditional retail core - repair and insurance services, a third-party marketplace, retail media advertising sold to suppliers, private label, and renting floor space - from 31% three years ago to 33%, then 36%, and 'approximately 40%' by the half year to March 2026, calling it 'a EUR 1 billion business'. Retail media income 'nearly doubled' in the first half. These are supplier-funded, capital-light income streams that only a retailer with 57 million loyalty members and a marketplace covering 98% of the footprint can sell, and they carry structurally better margins than selling televisions. If that mix keeps shifting, the company's earnings power is materially higher than the 15.1% gross margin of the legacy business suggests.

The delivery record supports the target. The EUR 500 million adjusted operating profit goal set at the 2023 Capital Markets Day has been repeated 'precisely to the last decimal' and reiterated at all three calls under review. The first quarter delivered EUR 311 million against a disclosed seasonal shape of 64% / 6% / 1% / 29% - an unusually specific and testable disclosure - and the third quarter did not break it. Three of the nine strategic indicators were hit ahead of their September 2026 deadline. Poland, the problem market, was visibly fixed with a new local chief executive and chief financial officer and two consecutive quarters of profit improvement.

The balance sheet is better than the headline suggests. The scan's EUR 1.51 billion of net debt is a lease-inclusive figure struck at a retailer's seasonal cash trough; strip out roughly EUR 1.7 billion of capitalised leases and the company carries close to zero net financial debt, arguably a small net cash position, against EUR 1.09 billion of cash. The negative cash conversion cycle of about minus 34 days means growth funds itself.

Finally, the ownership structure caps the downside in a way an ordinary micro-cap's does not. JD.com holds 85.2% and has already stated a strategic value of EUR 4.60 per share in cash. All merger clearances are done, Italian and German foreign-investment approvals are granted, and JD.com has offered remedies to Brussels. If the transaction closes, German exchange law obliges a delisting purchase offer at no less than the six-month volume-weighted average price, and any subsequent domination agreement or squeeze-out requires compensation set by independent valuation and reviewable by a German court - a mechanism that has historically paid minority holders at or above the strategic buyer's own price.

Conditions this case depends on: (1) the European Commission clears the transaction on or before its 2 October 2026 deadline, or the parties extend past the 10 November 2026 long-stop; (2) the EUR 500 million adjusted profit target lands in the September 2026 year-end; (3) the growth businesses keep compounding their share of gross profit; and (4) an investor can actually transact in a share where 85.2% is locked up.
bear_thesis:
The bear case has three legs, and the first is that the headline cheapness is largely an accounting artefact. Every number management is judged on is an adjusted number. Trailing operating profit as reported is about EUR 135 million; trailing operating profit before depreciation is EUR 782 million; the 2025/26 adjusted target implies roughly EUR 1.15 billion on the same basis. That is a gap of some EUR 365 million a year between what is presented and what is filed, at a company whose entire equity is worth about EUR 1.9 billion. The chief financial officer only conceded the bridge when a journalist pushed in December 2025 - 'what is causing the EBIT to be negative is the investment... in the JD Corporation, EUR 32 million... and also the Poland restructuring'. A retailer that has restructured Poland, closed and reformatted German stores and is modernising '360 stores... by the end of next year' is one for which restructuring is a permanent line item, not an exception. Capitalise the adjusted number and you are capitalising a choice.

The second leg is that the returns are poor and the multiple is not actually cheap against the right peer. Return on invested capital is 1.8%, the net margin is essentially zero (2025 net income minus EUR 35 million, 2023 minus EUR 39 million), tangible book value is negative, book value per share has fallen 15.7% a year over five years, and the Altman solvency score of 2.29 sits in the grey zone. Gross margin is 15.1% and contracting - a wide moat shows up as pricing power in the gross margin, and it is not there. On live enterprise value to trailing profit before depreciation, CECONOMY trades at 4.4 times against Currys at 4.5 times: the closest true comparable, essentially in line. The apparent discount to Fnac Darty at 6.8 times and Best Buy at 8.6 times is earned by a materially worse return profile, not mispriced.

The third and most immediate leg is that the share is a regulatory binary that a market buyer cannot hedge and cannot capture. The EUR 4.60 takeover offer's acceptance period closed on 10 November 2025 - shares bought today cannot be tendered into it, and JD.com's 85.2% sits below the 95% at which German law would grant a sell-out right at the offer price. The European Commission opened an in-depth foreign-subsidies investigation on 28 May 2026, issued formal objections in July 2026, and must decide by 2 October 2026. On 19 August 2026 China's Ministry of Justice directed domestic entities not to support that investigation, calling it unlawful and extraterritorial - meaning the party whose information the Commission requires has been ordered by its own government not to provide it, in a proceeding where failure to supply information is itself grounds for prohibition. Should the deal fail, the reference point is the undisturbed price implied by the offer's own disclosure: EUR 4.60 was a 42.6% premium to the three-month average as of 23 July 2025, implying about EUR 3.23 before the bid, with a governance vacuum, a newly installed chief executive, and the re-emergence of large pre-existing holders as sellers.

Even winning the binary pays little. Management guided delisting at 'between 3 and 6 months after closing', and German exchange law prices a delisting purchase offer at no less than the six-month volume-weighted average - which on the current band (50-day average EUR 3.92, 200-day EUR 4.21) is roughly EUR 4.00 to 4.15, not EUR 4.60. Anything better requires a domination agreement or squeeze-out whose court-reviewed compensation lands years later, in a share that by then no longer trades. And liquidity is already gone: about 19,400 shares changed hands on 24 August 2026, roughly EUR 77,000 of turnover.

What would confirm the bear case: a Commission prohibition or a withdrawn notification on or before 2 October 2026; the 10 November 2026 long-stop passing without an extension; a September 2026 year-end that misses the EUR 500 million adjusted target; or a delisting purchase offer announced at or below EUR 4.15.
consensus_delta:
Where we disagree with the market is not about the business - it is about what a share of it entitles you to.

The visible market framing, and the one most retail commentary repeats, is that CECONOMY trades at EUR 3.94 against a EUR 4.60 takeover price and therefore carries roughly 17% of merger upside. That framing is factually wrong. The acceptance period for JD.com's EUR 4.60 cash offer closed on 10 November 2025. Shares bought on the market today cannot be tendered into it. JD.com's 85.2% holding sits below the 95% at which German takeover law would give the remaining holders a statutory right to sell at the offer price. There is no contractual claim on EUR 4.60 for anyone buying now. What a buyer actually owns is a claim on whatever mechanism JD.com uses to take the company private, and management has told us what that is: delisting 'between 3 and 6 months after closing'. German exchange law prices a delisting purchase offer at no less than the six-month volume-weighted average price - which, with the shares having traded between EUR 3.51 and EUR 4.59 and averaging EUR 3.92 over 50 days and EUR 4.21 over 200 days, is roughly EUR 4.00 to 4.15. The best plausible near-term outcome is therefore a few percent, not seventeen.

The second incorrect assumption is that all regulatory risk is behind the deal. It is a natural inference from the sequence of good news - all merger clearances obtained, Italian approval in February, German foreign-investment approval with conditions in July 2026 - and management encouraged it, saying on 13 May 2026 that they 'remain confident across all necessary approvals'. But the binding constraint was never merger control. It is the Foreign Subsidies Regulation, where the Commission issued formal objections in July 2026 and must decide by 2 October 2026, and where on 19 August 2026 China's Ministry of Justice ordered domestic entities not to cooperate. This is the precise failure mode our current regime read flags: a transaction can clear every merger authority on earth and still be stopped by a single non-merger process. Clearance-count-based deal-risk models are mis-specified here.

The third disagreement runs the other way, in the company's favour, and it is why this is a pass rather than a short. The market's own valuation of the operating business is not obviously wrong. At 4.4 times enterprise value to trailing profit before depreciation, CECONOMY sits level with Currys at 4.5 times. There is no large idiosyncratic relative-value gap to harvest; the low multiple is paid for with a 1.8% return on invested capital, a zero net margin, and a contracting 15.1% gross margin. The one genuinely under-appreciated fact is operating: third-quarter revenue to 30 June 2026 grew 9.8% year on year and the reported operating loss halved, on filed rather than adjusted numbers. But that improvement is worth perhaps a point of multiple in a share nobody can trade, not a re-rating.

Net: the street is not looking the wrong way about the business. A significant part of the retail audience is looking the wrong way about the instrument - reading a spread that no longer exists.
forcing_function:
Three dated events, in sequence.

**2 October 2026 - the European Commission's decision deadline** on the foreign-subsidies investigation opened 28 May 2026. This is the hard one and it is binary. Clearance, with or without the remedies JD.com has offered, removes the largest discount in the price. Prohibition returns the shares toward the pre-bid EUR 3.23 implied by the offer's own 42.6% premium disclosure as of 23 July 2025.

**10 November 2026 - the contractual long-stop date,** reported unchanged as of 20 August 2026. If the Commission has not decided, this forces either an extension - which opens a renegotiation in which EUR 4.60 could be reset lower given the shares trade below it - or termination.

**Closing plus three to six months - the delisting purchase offer.** Management stated on 13 May 2026 that delisting follows 'between 3 and 6 months' after completion. German exchange law requires the offer to be priced at no less than the six-month volume-weighted average price, currently roughly EUR 4.00 to 4.15 on a 50-day average of EUR 3.92 and a 200-day average of EUR 4.21. This is the event that actually converts a shareholding into cash, and it is the one that caps the realistic near-term return at low single digits.

Beyond those, the residual and much slower forcing function is a domination and profit-transfer agreement or a squeeze-out. JD.com's 85.2% comfortably exceeds the 75% needed to pass a domination agreement at a shareholder meeting but falls short of the 95% required for a squeeze-out. A domination agreement would oblige JD.com to offer both a guaranteed annual dividend and an exit compensation set by independent valuation and reviewable by a German court - the only route by which a buyer at today's price plausibly realises materially more than the delisting offer. It is also the slowest: measured in years, in a security that will no longer trade, with the compensation set by a valuer appointed under a process the minority holder does not control.

There is one further scheduled event of secondary importance: fiscal year-end on 30 September 2026, when the entire 2023 Capital Markets Day target set comes due, including the EUR 500 million adjusted operating profit goal. It matters for the valuation input into any later compensation calculation more than it matters for the share price.
valley_of_death:
The next three to nine months contain the entire question, and the sequencing is unusually cruel.

First, 2 October 2026: the European Commission's deadline on the foreign-subsidies investigation. Formal objections were already issued in July 2026 and JD.com has offered remedies. A prohibition, or a withdrawal-and-refile that resets the clock past the long-stop, is the single event that takes these shares toward the pre-bid level near EUR 3.23 - a drop of roughly a fifth from here, and plausibly worse in the first days given how thin the float is.

Second, and compounding it, the 19 August 2026 directive from China's Ministry of Justice ordering domestic entities not to support the investigation. This is not ordinary regulatory friction. Under the Foreign Subsidies Regulation the Commission may decide adversely where required information is not supplied. JD.com is now caught between two states, and the company cannot resolve that by negotiating harder in Brussels. This risk sits entirely outside management's control and outside anything in the financial statements.

Third, 10 November 2026: the contractual long-stop. Reported unchanged as of 20 August 2026. If the Commission has not decided by then, the parties must either extend - a renegotiation window in which the EUR 4.60 reference could be reset lower, since the shares now trade below it - or the agreement lapses.

Fourth, the fiscal year ends 30 September 2026 and with it the entire 2023 Capital Markets Day target set. The EUR 500 million adjusted operating profit target requires the fourth quarter to deliver about 29% of the year on management's own disclosed seasonal shape. Nine of the nine strategic indicators come due on the same date, and only three were reported achieved. A miss lands into a market already jumpy about the deal.

There is, importantly, no financing cliff. The company is close to net-cash on financial debt excluding leases, holds EUR 1.09 billion of cash, generated EUR 337 million of free cash flow in 2024/25, and runs a negative cash conversion cycle that funds growth. The Altman solvency score of 2.29 is grey-zone rather than distressed. The valley here is entirely event-driven, not liquidity-driven - which is why the drawdown, if it comes, will be a single gap rather than a grind.

One further hazard specific to this name: the fourth-quarter results and any post-close corporate actions may be communicated into a shrinking public shareholder base with reduced reporting obligations. Management explicitly warned in the offer documentation that non-accepting shareholders face 'reduced liquidity and limited financial reporting'. The information environment gets worse from here, not better.
positioning_washout:
The washout has already happened, and that is precisely the problem - it removed the shareholders and left the shares.

JD.com holds 85.2% following the offer that closed on 10 November 2025: 59.8% tendered plus Convergenta's 25.4%, with irrevocable commitments from Haniel, freenet and the Beisheim Stiftung. Every strategic and family holder is out. What remains is a free float of roughly 15%, and the trading evidence is stark: about 19,400 shares changed hands on 24 August 2026, some EUR 77,000 of turnover in a company with EUR 23.8 billion of revenue. This is not a position any real book can build or exit at size, and that alone disqualifies it before any view on value.

The mechanical selling still ahead is index-driven and one-directional. CECONOMY has already left Germany's mid-cap index in substance through the collapse of its free float; on a completed delisting, every remaining index and exchange-traded fund holder must sell, and does so into a market with no natural buyer other than JD.com itself. Delisting is guided at 'between 3 and 6 months after closing'. Institutional mandates that prohibit unlisted holdings will be forced sellers on a known date into known thin liquidity - a structure that historically prints below the delisting offer price, not above it.

There is no dividend-driven washout to look for: the stated 15-25% payout policy has been reaffirmed but is inert because net income is negative, so there is no yield-focused base to flush. Goldman Sachs was reported building to 4.56% ahead of the 18 February 2026 shareholder meeting, which reads as an event book positioning for a compensation process rather than a fundamental holder - a shareholder base that will not defend the price on bad news.

The asymmetry of this positioning picture is unattractive. There is no forced-selling dislocation left to buy, because the forced selling already cleared into JD.com's hands at EUR 4.60. What is left is forced selling still to come, at whatever the delisting mechanism sets.
moderator_conclusion:
Pass for now. The business is better than its reputation; the security is worse than its headline.

Start with the mistake this file exists to avoid. CECONOMY does not trade at a 17% discount to a EUR 4.60 takeover offer in any sense a buyer can collect. That offer's acceptance window shut on 10 November 2025, and JD.com's 85.2% sits below the 95% at which German law would grant remaining holders a right to sell at the offer price. A share bought at EUR 3.94 today carries no contractual claim on EUR 4.60. What it carries is a claim on a statutory delisting purchase offer priced at the six-month volume-weighted average - roughly EUR 4.00 to 4.15 on current trading - plus a long, slow option on court-set compensation in a domination agreement or squeeze-out years later. Best realistic near-term case: a few percent. That single fact reframes everything.

Against that thin upside sits a genuinely wide-tailed downside. The European Commission's foreign-subsidies decision is due 2 October 2026, formal objections were already issued in July 2026, and on 19 August 2026 China's Ministry of Justice ordered domestic entities not to cooperate with the investigation - a party being told by its own state not to supply information in a proceeding where non-supply is itself grounds for prohibition. If the deal breaks, the offer's own disclosure gives the reference: EUR 4.60 was a 42.6% premium to the three-month average as of 23 July 2025, implying about EUR 3.23 undisturbed. Roughly a fifth of downside against a few percent of realistic upside is the wrong shape.

The current regime read reinforces this rather than fighting it. Merger-arb has been demoted to fourth of the special situation lanes precisely because clean spreads are picked over and the tail got worse: the Paramount case cleared every federal and 68 foreign regulators and was frozen anyway by a non-merger process, and the standing instruction is to 'underwrite the legal event, never the spread'. Underwriting the legal event here means underwriting an EU-China geopolitical dispute in which neither party is the company. It is also the opposite of resolution-driver independence: the entire thesis rides one shared political factor. There is no rate-rescue or Fed-cut dependency here, which is to its credit, but there is a single non-diversifiable binary. The regime's preference for cash-generating businesses does apply and CECONOMY superficially qualifies at 2.7 times price to free cash flow - but the trailing EUR 731 million is working-capital flattered, and management's own steady-state guide is EUR 200 million a year.

Now judge the residual value case on its own, ignoring the event entirely, as this book requires. The operating turn is real and it is in the filed numbers, not just the adjusted ones: third-quarter revenue to 30 June 2026 up 9.8% year on year, the reported operating loss halved from minus EUR 82 million to minus EUR 44 million, free cash flow of EUR 337 million in 2024/25, and the share of gross profit from services, marketplace, retail media, private label and space rental up from 31% to about 40% in three years. Management's forensic record is good on the metrics it chooses to guide - the EUR 500 million target repeated unchanged across three calls and tracking, a disclosed quarterly profit shape it can be held to, Poland visibly fixed. That earns a credibility score of four.

But the value case does not clear the bar. On live multiples CECONOMY trades at 4.4 times enterprise value to trailing profit before depreciation against Currys at 4.5 - level with its closest true comparable, not cheap. The wider gap to Fnac Darty and Best Buy is earned by a 1.8% return on invested capital, a zero net margin, negative tangible book value, and a gross margin of 15.1% that is contracting. And roughly EUR 365 million a year separates presented profit from filed profit at a company worth EUR 1.9 billion - restructuring treated as exceptional by a retailer that restructures continuously. Our sum-of-the-parts, giving management credit for about half that bridge, lands at EUR 4.50 against a price of EUR 3.94. Fourteen percent of upside to fair value, on a business earning 1.8% on capital, is not a value proposition; it is fair pricing. Hence a value score of two, entirely independent of the catalyst.

The moat is narrow and, unusually, stable rather than eroding: the retail core's product margin is deteriorating, but the higher-margin income streams are offsetting it at pace, so the durable profit pool is holding. Retail channel shift is a material structural threat, not a terminal one - this company is monetising the shift through its marketplace and retail media rather than only suffering it. That keeps it out of value-trap territory and off the moat cap.

The final and decisive point is practical. With 85.2% locked up, roughly 19,400 shares traded on 24 August 2026 - about EUR 77,000. A real book cannot build a position, cannot exit one, and would be holding an untraded security within a year of any successful close. Even a correct call here cannot be expressed. Pass, and if the transaction is prohibited and the shares reset toward EUR 3.20 with a standalone company guiding EUR 500 million of adjusted operating profit and a re-floated register, this becomes a genuinely interesting file to reopen.

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC

The story management tells has been remarkably stable across the three calls, and that stability is itself the finding. **One correction to the screener's balance sheet.** The input block reports net debt of **1.51bn** at 30 June 2026 and instructs that it be treated as a liability, which is right. But the composition matters: the March 2026 balance sheet separates **1.68bn of capitalised lease obligations** from roughly **0.9bn of actual borrowings**. Against **1.09bn of cash**, CECONOMY carries **near-zero net financial debt** — arguably a small net cash position — and the 1.51bn figure is a lease-inclusive number struck at the seasonal low point of a retailer's cash cycle. The sum-of-the-parts below uses the **lease-inclusive 1.51bn**, which is the conservative choice and the one consistent with valuing the business on profit measured after lease depreciation.

---

## 3. TONE & CONFIDENCE TRAJECTORY

**Rising on operations, tightening on the deal.**

- **December 2025:** expansive and personal. "I'm more convinced than ever that this partnership will make us even stronger." Specific, checkable operational detail: 16 regional fulfilment centres, 8.8 weeks of stock reach, a 37% online-order pickup rate.
- **February 2026:** more confident still, and notably more numerate. The quarter is framed as "a stress test... and we have successfully completed that stress test." The chief financial officer volunteered the quarterly profit shape to the percentage point — an offensive move, since it hands analysts a stick to measure him with.
- **May 2026:** the operational voice is unchanged and if anything warmer, but the register splits. On the business: "we must not get and we are not arrogant." On regulation, the language goes flat and legal: "I cannot comment on ongoing discussions", "I cannot give you any color on this."

There is no drift from growth language to cost language — both are present throughout, and the cost programme is framed as a response to a named regional softness rather than a defensive pivot. The one genuinely defensive note is Germany, where the answer has become an action plan rather than a description.

---

## 4. GUIDANCE CREDIBILITY

**Score: High, with one qualification.**

The delivery record on the metrics management chooses to guide is good. Full-year 2024/25 sales came in above the "moderate growth" they had guided. The 500m adjusted operating profit target set at the 2023 Capital Markets Day has been repeated "precisely to the last decimal since" and, three quarters in, is tracking. Three of the nine strategic key indicators were hit ahead of the September 2026 deadline. The screener's beat rate of two of the last three quarters is consistent.

Two behaviours cut the other way. First, management refuses to refresh stale targets: asked directly to update the Capital Markets Day cash-flow and margin goals, the chief financial officer answered "we will not comment on numbers in any detail" and then reaffirmed a three-year-old 200m cash-flow figure that the business has already beaten. That is convenient in both directions — it protects the downside and denies analysts an updated bar. Second, and more seriously, every headline they are judged on is an adjusted one. Guidance credibility on adjusted profit is high; guidance credibility on reported profit has never been tested, because they have never given it. When a journalist asked for reported guidance in December, the answer was a restatement of the adjusted target.

---

## 5. ANALYST PRESSURE POINTS

- **The regulatory clock.** Asked repeatedly and by name — the EU foreign-subsidies review, the Austrian foreign-investment approval, whether remedies would be required — management gave three consecutive non-answers, the most explicit being to a hedge fund analyst in May: "these are very sensitive discussions, the confidentiality of which we respect 100%." This has since turned into bad news (see section 8).
- **What minority holders actually get.** The one question that matters most to a buyer of these shares today — the delisting mechanism and price — was asked in May and answered only on timing: "between 3 and 6 months after closing... I can't give you a precise timing." No price, no mechanism, no reference to a compensation offer.
- **Germany.** Asked in both February and May why German costs are so high and whether more stores close. The answer moved from a benchmarking programme to "at the moment, we don't" plan further closures — a formulation that leaves the door open.
- **Reported versus adjusted.** Asked once, in December, by a journalist rather than an analyst. Nobody has pushed on the 365m annual gap. That is the question the sell side is not asking.
- **What happens after September 2026.** The current target set expires with this fiscal year and the successor plan was deferred to a July strategy day that lands inside a live takeover. Analysts noticed: "is there any meaningful EBIT and margin upside that can carry over beyond '25, '26?" The answer — "we don't believe that EUR 500 million is the ceiling here and everything else will need to be set in July" — is the least specific statement in three calls.

---

## 6. RED FLAGS / GREEN FLAGS

🔴 **Every headline is an adjusted headline.** Roughly 365m a year of charges sits between the presented profit and the filed profit, at a company whose entire equity value is about 1.9bn.

🔴 **Returns do not support the narrative.** Twelve quarters of adjusted profit growth have produced a 1.8% return on invested capital, a negative net margin, negative tangible book value, and a five-year decline in book value per share of 15.7% a year.

🔴 **Gross margin is contracting** (15.1% and falling) even as the higher-margin add-on businesses grow — meaning the retail core's product margin is deteriorating faster than the new businesses are offsetting it.

🔴 **Chief executive turnover mid-transaction.** May 2026 was Kai-Ulrich Deissner's "14th, but also my last earnings call"; the chief financial officer, Remko Rijnders, succeeds him. Losing the architect of the transformation while the transaction is unapproved is not ideal timing.

🔴 **Regulatory answers went dark** between December and May while the guided closing slipped from the first half of 2026 to the second.

🟢 **The operating turn is real and it is accelerating.** Third-quarter revenue to 30 June 2026 rose **9.8%** year on year, and the reported operating loss in a structurally loss-making quarter halved from minus 82m to minus 44m. That is a genuine, filed, unadjusted improvement.

🟢 **The mix shift is measurable, not rhetorical.** Share of gross profit from services, marketplace, retail media, private label and space rental went 31% → 33% → 36% → 40% across the disclosed periods. Retail media income "nearly doubled" in the first half.

🟢 **Cash generation is real** even after discounting the working-capital flattery: 337m of free cash flow in 2024/25, up 180%, against a company-guided steady state of 200m.

🟢 **Disclosure discipline is above average.** Volunteering the quarterly profit split (64/6/1/29) and publishing the same nine-indicator scorecard every quarter are the habits of a team that expects to be checked.

🟢 **Poland was fixed, visibly.** A new local chief executive and chief financial officer, a marketplace launch, and an operating-profit improvement confirmed in two consecutive quarters.

---

## 7. HIDDEN SIGNALS

- **"Growth businesses" became a reporting segment in all but name.** By May they have their own gross-profit bridge. When a company starts drawing a line down the middle of its own profit statement, it is either preparing a story about the good half or preparing to be valued on it.
- **The successor's voice is a cost voice.** Every operational answer on Germany, Poland and the profit bridge in the last two calls came from the chief financial officer, not the chief executive — benchmarking, indirect spend, location costs, "on par with the benchmark of our company." The incoming chief executive's instincts are visibly margin-and-cost rather than brand-and-experience. Expect the next plan to be flatter and more numerical than the outgoing one.
- **The Saturn question keeps coming back** and keeps getting the same emphatic non-denial: "we have 2 brands. Actually, if you're really picky, we have three... And it stays like that." Journalists do not repeat a question across quarters without a reason.
- **The dividend policy was reaffirmed but is inert.** A stated payout of 15–25% of net profit means nothing when net profit is negative. Reciting a policy that cannot pay is a way of avoiding saying there will be no dividend.
- **"Between 3 and 6 months after closing" for the delisting** was volunteered without prompting. Management has thought about the exit route for public shareholders in some detail; it simply will not say what they will be paid.

---

## 8. CAPITAL-ALLOCATION VERDICT (for the director)

**Trajectory: STRENGTHENING.** The operating business is genuinely better than it was two years ago on filed, unadjusted numbers — revenue growing, losses narrowing, cash generating, mix shifting toward higher-margin income, and a fixed public target that is tracking three quarters in. This is not a company in decline.

**The single most important thing to weigh before sizing: what a buyer of these shares can actually collect, and when.** This is not an ordinary equity any more. JD.com's takeover offer of **EUR 4.60 per share in cash** — a 42.6% premium to the three-month average price as of 23 July 2025, implying an undisturbed price near **EUR 3.23** — closed its acceptance window on **10 November 2025**. Shares bought on the market today **cannot be tendered into it.** JD.com holds **85.2%**, below the 95% at which German law would give minority holders a sell-out right at the offer price. So the 17% gap between today's EUR 3.94 and the EUR 4.60 headline is not a spread anyone can capture; it is the market pricing a different question entirely.

What remains is a chain of contingent events. The European Commission opened an in-depth foreign-subsidies investigation on **28 May 2026**, issued formal objections in **July 2026**, and must decide by **2 October 2026**; the contract's long-stop date is **10 November 2026**. JD.com has offered remedies. Against that, China's Ministry of Justice issued a directive on **19 August 2026** instructing domestic entities not to support the EU investigation, which Beijing calls unlawful and extraterritorial — a supplier of information being ordered by its own government not to supply it, in a proceeding where failure to supply information is itself grounds for prohibition. German foreign-investment approval came in July 2026 with data-protection conditions; Italian approval and all merger clearances are done. If the deal closes, management has said delisting follows "between 3 and 6 months", and German exchange law requires the delisting purchase offer to be priced at no less than the volume-weighted average price of the preceding six months — which, on the current trading band (50-day average EUR 3.92, 200-day EUR 4.21), is roughly **EUR 4.00–4.15**, not EUR 4.60. Anything better than that requires a later domination agreement or squeeze-out, where German law sets compensation by independent valuation subject to court review — a path measured in years, in a share that will by then be untraded.

The float is the other hard constraint: with 85.2% locked up, roughly **19,400 shares changed hands today**, about EUR 77,000 of turnover. This is not a position a real book can build or exit.

**Economic moat: NARROW.** The moat type is scale and intangible brand — Europe's largest consumer-electronics retail network across eleven countries, 57 million loyalty members, a marketplace carrying nearly four million items, and a supplier-funded retail-media business that only a retailer of this size can sell. Those are real advantages. But the evidence says narrow, not wide: **return on invested capital of 1.8%**, a **net margin of essentially zero**, and a **gross margin of 15.1% that is contracting.** A wide moat shows up as pricing power in the gross margin, and it is not there.

**Moat trend: STABLE.** Two forces are cancelling. The retail core's product margin is eroding, but the share of gross profit from higher-margin services, marketplace, retail media, private label and space rental has climbed from 31% to 40% in three years, and those businesses are growing at double-digit-to-doubling rates. Net, the durable profit pool is holding rather than widening or melting.

**Secular threat: MATERIAL, not terminal.** The structural force is retail channel shift — online-native marketplaces and direct-to-consumer brands taking share from big-box electronics floors. It is real, it is permanent, and it is why this sector trades where it does. But CECONOMY is not passively absorbing it: 30% of sales are already online, the marketplace covers 98% of the footprint, and the company is converting store space and customer data into advertising and services income — monetising the shift rather than only suffering it. The cheapness is therefore neither a pure fear-print nor a pure value trap. It is a fairly-priced, low-return business in a structurally pressured channel, whose share price is currently being set by a regulatory binary rather than by any of that.

Management credibility 4 of 5 · trajectory improving · a narrow but real moat · moat trend steady · structural threat material.

bull_thesis:
The bull case is that this is a genuinely improving European retailer being valued as a dying one, and that a controlling shareholder eventually has to pay to take out the 14.8% it does not own.

Start with the operating evidence, because it is stronger than the reputation. CECONOMY runs MediaMarkt and Saturn, roughly 1,000 consumer-electronics stores across 11 countries and about EUR 24 billion of annual sales. Management has now delivered twelve consecutive quarters of growth in adjusted operating profit, and the growth is accelerating rather than fading: the quarter to 30 June 2026 produced sales of EUR 5,273 million against EUR 4,803 million a year earlier, up 9.8% and the fastest rate in the series, with the net loss narrowing to EUR 66 million from EUR 114 million. Full-year guidance of around EUR 500 million of adjusted operating profit was reaffirmed on 13 May 2026, and the December-2025 quarter delivered EUR 311 million of it, matching the 64% seasonal share the chief financial officer said that quarter should carry.

The substantive change underneath is a mix shift that management measures rather than asserts. What they call growth businesses, meaning retail media (selling advertising to suppliers against store traffic and customer data), services and solutions, a third-party marketplace, private label and rented floor space, moved from 31% of gross profit in fiscal 2022/23 to about 40% in the half year to March 2026, with retail-media income nearly doubling and the marketplace live across 98% of the footprint after the January 2026 Switzerland launch. These lines carry structurally higher margins than selling boxes and are far less exposed to the electronics replacement cycle. Online is 30% of sales at its peak and growing 7-8% a year, and 37% of online orders are collected in a store, so the company is participating in the channel shift rather than being bypassed by it.

The balance sheet is stronger than the headline implies. Reported net debt of EUR 1,506 million at 30 June 2026 is almost entirely capitalised store rent; the March-2026 balance sheet shows EUR 1,678 million of the EUR 2.7 billion of total debt was lease liabilities, so on a pre-lease basis the company sits close to net cash. Working capital is financed by suppliers, with a cash conversion cycle of negative 34 days and inventory down to 8.8 weeks of stock reach.

The ownership structure is the asymmetric part. JD.com holds 85.2%. That is above the 75% at which German law permits a domination and profit-transfer agreement, which obliges the controlling company to offer minorities a cash exit valued on the company's intrinsic worth and subject to court review in appraisal proceedings that historically settle above the market price. It is below the 95% at which minorities can simply be bought out. A holder at EUR 3.975 therefore owns a claim on whatever process JD eventually chooses, in a company a strategic buyer valued at EUR 4.60 a share in July 2025. On a parts basis the enterprise is worth about EUR 4.7 billion in the favourable case, roughly EUR 6.50 a share after debt.

The conditions this requires: the EUR 500 million adjusted operating target is delivered on 30 September 2026 and the roughly EUR 300 million of annual charges below it finally stops recurring; German demand stabilises; the pending European and national approvals clear so JD closes; and JD then chooses a route that pays minorities rather than leaving a stub outstanding indefinitely.
bear_thesis:
The bear case is not that the business fails. It is that the security is mismeasured, fairly priced, and structurally on the wrong side of its controlling shareholder.

The measurement error comes first, because it is what put this name on the screen. The screening record reads a price-to-free-cash-flow multiple of 2.9 times and a trailing free cash flow of EUR 731 million. Under current lease accounting, store rent is stripped out of operating cash flow and reappears in financing: those payments ran about EUR 524 million across the last four quarters. Net of them, free cash flow available to the equity is roughly EUR 207 million, which is 9.6 times the EUR 1.93 billion market value, not 2.9 times. Management's own guidance corroborates the corrected number almost exactly: on 17 December 2025 the chief financial officer reaffirmed the 2023 capital-markets-day target of 'a stable cash flow of EUR 200 million per year, and we're also not changing that number'. The company is telling you the real figure while the screen reads three and a half times it.

The second problem is that the profit being celebrated is not the profit being earned. In 2024/25 an adjusted operating profit of EUR 378 million sat on top of a negative reported operating result. In 2025/26 the adjusted figure is guided to around EUR 500 million while reported operating profit is tracking toward roughly EUR 200 million. That is a gap of about EUR 300 million a year, three years running, attributed each year to a different named one-off: JD transaction costs of EUR 32 million and Polish restructuring in December 2025, German restructuring in May 2026. An add-back that appears every year is a cost. The reported record is unambiguous: net income of negative EUR 39 million in 2023, positive EUR 76 million in 2024, negative EUR 35 million in 2025, and trailing diluted earnings per share of negative EUR 0.03. Return on invested capital is 1.8%. Interest expense of about EUR 252 million a year consumes half the guided adjusted operating profit before a shareholder sees anything.

The third problem is that there is no discount to capture. Checked live on 31 August 2026, CECONOMY trades at 4.39 times enterprise value to operating cash profit against Currys plc, its closest listed comparable, at 4.55 times. The gap to Best Buy at 7.46 times is earned rather than a mispricing: Best Buy returns 17.2% on invested capital, CECONOMY 1.8%.

The fourth and largest problem is the structure. The acceptance window on JD's EUR 4.60 offer closed on 10 November 2025 and cannot reopen. A share bought today carries no claim on that price. JD holds 85.2%, controls the board, the guidance and the disclosure calendar, and would set any statutory delisting purchase offer at the trailing six-month volume-weighted average price, currently around EUR 4.05 and falling as the share price falls. Its economic interest is served by a low share price for as long as the exit is undecided. Meanwhile the free float is 14.8% and liquidity has evaporated: 6,252 shares changed hands on 31 August 2026, roughly EUR 25,000 for a whole session. There is no dividend, despite a policy reaffirmed in December 2025, because the payout ratio is applied to a net profit of approximately zero.

What would confirm the bear case: a European foreign-subsidies or national foreign-investment decision that blocks or conditions the transaction, leaving an 85.2% holder stranded above an illiquid stub; a September-2026 result that misses the EUR 500 million target; another year in which several hundred million euros of charges are declared exceptional; or simply nothing at all happening, which costs a holder the time value with no dividend to wait on. The December-2025 quarter already carried a warning that went unremarked: gross margin in the seasonally dominant quarter fell 184 basis points, to 15.08% from 16.92%, while the presentation led with a record online share and a record customer-satisfaction score.
consensus_delta:
The market is not looking the wrong way here. Our own screen was.

The usual shape of a disagreement in this book is that the street prices terminal decline into a business with stable or growing earnings power. That is not the situation. The street prices CECONOMY at 4.39 times enterprise value to operating cash profit and prices Currys plc, the same business model in a neighbouring market, at 4.55 times, both checked live on 31 August 2026. The market has looked at two European box retailers and given them the same number. That is a considered judgement, not neglect.

Where we do disagree is with our own inputs, and the correction cuts against the position rather than for it. Three assumptions embedded in the screening record are wrong.

First, the price-to-free-cash-flow multiple of 2.9 times and the trailing free cash flow of EUR 731 million. Under current lease accounting, store rent is removed from operating cash flow and reappears in financing; those payments totalled about EUR 524 million over the last four quarters. Free cash flow to the equity is therefore about EUR 207 million and the multiple is about 9.6 times. Management guides to the corrected number in public: on 17 December 2025 the chief financial officer reaffirmed 'a stable cash flow of EUR 200 million per year'. The company has been telling anyone who listens what the real figure is.

Second, the discounted-cash-flow fair value of EUR 19.6 carried on the stock page, and the associated margin-of-safety readings of plus 79% on discounted cash flow, plus 76% on owner earnings and plus 58% on earnings power. All four are computed off the uncorrected cash-flow figure and are therefore inflated by roughly three and a half times at the input. A fair value five times the traded price for a retailer earning 1.8% on invested capital should have been rejected on sight. Notably, the two methods that read minus 100%, the Graham and the fifteen-times-intrinsic screens, are the ones anchored to reported earnings, and reported earnings are approximately zero. The disagreement between our own methods was the signal.

Third, the implied claim on EUR 4.60. It does not exist. JD.com's offer window closed on 10 November 2025 and the shares trade 13.6% below that price for the good reason that no holder can collect it.

Where we do hold a modest non-consensus view, it is on the business rather than the security, and it is not enough to buy. The market appears to treat this as a structurally shrinking electronics retailer, and it is not one: sales grew 9.8% in the quarter to 30 June 2026, the growth businesses moved from 31% to about 40% of gross profit in three years, and retail-media income nearly doubled in the half year to March 2026. Retail media in particular monetises store traffic and first-party customer data that a pure online competitor cannot reach. That argues the business is worth roughly EUR 4.45 a share rather than EUR 3.975. It is a 12% disagreement, not an investable one.

One street assumption we would flag as genuinely unexamined, because nobody asked it on any of the three calls in the file: what a minority holder is entitled to receive. No analyst asked what price a delisting purchase offer would be struck at, or whether a domination agreement is contemplated. The absence of that question is the clearest evidence that the remaining float is not being underwritten by anybody.
forcing_function:
There are two candidate forcing functions and, honestly assessed, neither delivers the money to a holder buying today.

The first is dated and hard, and it belongs to somebody else. On the 13 May 2026 call the chief executive named 10 November 2026 as the long-stop date for the JD.com transaction, saying completion was expected 'in the second half of the calendar year, but obviously before November 10, which is the long stop date'. That date is binding on JD and CECONOMY. It is not a payment to a minority shareholder. Completion transfers control that JD already exercises at 85.2%; outside holders receive nothing on that day.

The second is the one that would actually pay, and it is neither dated nor promised. German law gives a controlling shareholder three routes past a minority. At 95% it can compel a buy-out; JD is at 85.2%, nearly five percentage points short, and would have to buy roughly 23 million shares in the market to get there, which in a stock trading 6,252 shares a day is not a quiet operation. Above 75%, which JD cleared long ago, it may put a domination and profit-transfer agreement to a shareholder meeting; that obliges it to offer minorities an annual guaranteed payment and a cash exit valued on the company's intrinsic worth, reviewable by a court in appraisal proceedings that historically settle above the offered figure. That is the genuinely asymmetric outcome for a holder here. And a delisting purchase offer would be struck at the trailing six-month volume-weighted average price, which we estimate at roughly EUR 4.05 today, about 2% above the current quote.

Management's own words on the timing of the third route are the best evidence available and they are deliberately vague: a delisting 'between 3 and 6 months after closing', immediately qualified with 'that's part of, not 100% easy process. So I can't give you a precise timing.' No domination agreement has been announced. No accumulation toward 95% has been disclosed to us.

The operating forcing function is real but small: the fiscal year ends 30 September 2026, when the EUR 500 million adjusted operating profit target and all nine key performance indicators from the 2023 capital-markets day come due, with results due around December 2026. A clean delivery would validate the mix shift. But the market has already told us how much it cares. The 9 July 2026 strategy day, at which management said the next phase would be set out and that 'we don't believe that EUR 500 million is the ceiling', moved the shares to EUR 4.20 on 147,766 units and was fully given back the following session at EUR 3.88. When the plan presentation round-trips in a day, the operating story is not what is holding the price.

The honest summary: the only event that re-rates this security is a decision by JD.com to pay for the rest of the company, and JD has no obligation to make it, no announced intention to make it, and a direct economic interest in the share price staying low until it does.
valley_of_death:
There is no cash-burn hump and no maturity wall here. The risks over the next three to nine months are the ordinary kind, plus one structural trap that is specific to this security.

Solvency is not the concern. At 30 June 2026 the company held EUR 1,091 million of cash against EUR 2,597 million of total debt, of which roughly EUR 1.7 billion is capitalised store rent rather than borrowing; on a pre-lease basis it sits close to net cash. Suppliers finance the working capital, with a cash conversion cycle of negative 34 days, and capital spending is trivial at about EUR 33 million a quarter against EUR 168 million of depreciation. The financial-strength score of 2.3 on the standard bankruptcy screen looks alarming and is a false reading for a negative-working-capital retailer.

What can go wrong, in order of likelihood.

The first is the seasonal cash swing, which is violent and will be misread. Net debt was nil at 31 December 2025, EUR 1,596 million at 31 March 2026 and EUR 1,506 million at 30 June 2026. The March quarter alone showed a EUR 1,483 million cash outflow as the Christmas payables unwound. Anyone marking this position on a quarterly balance sheet without adjusting for the cycle will see leverage appearing and disappearing that is not real.

The second is the fiscal year ending 30 September 2026, which is the moment the three-year plan comes due. Management set a EUR 500 million adjusted operating profit target at the 2023 capital-markets day and has repeated it 'precisely to the last decimal since'. Nine of nine key indicators fall due on that date. Two things could disappoint. The German and Austrian markets have been described as soft on both the February and May calls, with the region starting the year 'slightly below expectation from an EBIT perspective, mainly driven by top line', and Germany is roughly a third of the business. And the target is measured on the adjusted figure; the reported figure has run about EUR 300 million lower every year for three years, so hitting the target and reporting another near-zero net profit are entirely compatible outcomes.

The third is the regulatory tail on the JD transaction, which the current market regime says to take more seriously than usual. As of 13 May 2026 foreign-investment approvals were still outstanding in Austria, Germany and Spain, and the European foreign-subsidies review in Brussels was described only as constructive discussions. The regime read of 18 August 2026 is explicit that clearance-based deal-risk models are now mis-specified: Paramount's transaction satisfied every regulatory condition and cleared 68 countries and is frozen regardless, to a 2027 trial. A Chinese buyer of European retail infrastructure and customer data faces exactly the kind of political review that does not resolve on a schedule. The 10 November 2026 long-stop date falls inside the nine-month window.

The fourth, and the one that has no natural end, is that nothing happens. There is no dividend. The shares have de-rated from EUR 4.49 on 20 March 2026 to EUR 3.975, drifting down through a summer in which the operating results improved. A holder waiting for a controlling shareholder to decide receives nothing for waiting.

The fifth is liquidity itself. On 31 August 2026 the shares traded 6,252 units, roughly EUR 25,000 for a session. In an adverse tape, this is a security in which the exit is priced, not offered.
positioning_washout:
The forced selling has already happened, which is precisely why there is no washout left to buy.

The shareholder base was reshaped in one move. JD.com's tender took it to 85.2% by the end of November 2025, and every institution that wanted the offer price took it. What remains is a 14.8% float of roughly 72 million shares, worth about EUR 285 million. On 31 August 2026 that float turned over 6,252 shares.

The shares traded EUR 4.49 on 20 March and EUR 4.26 on 30 March on 436,130 shares, the heaviest session in the six months of data reviewed, and never recovered the level. We do not have a source naming the cause and will not assert one, but the flow is real and it is behind us, not ahead of us.

The 200-day average of EUR 4.198 sitting above the 50-day average of EUR 3.939 confirms the trend is down, not washed out.

The weighted diluted count was 502.8 million in the December-2025 quarter against 485.2 million basic, implying a convertible instrument that would dilute existing holders by roughly 3.6% if it converts. That is small, but in a stub with no float it is a real overhang.

# CECONOMY AG (CEC.DE) — Forensic Interrogator Dossier
**Date of review:** 31 August 2026 · **Price used:** EUR 3.975 (XETRA close, 31 Aug 2026) · **Market value:** about EUR 1.93 billion
**Transcripts reviewed:** 17 December 2025 (full-year 2024/25), 11 February 2026 (first quarter 2025/26), 13 May 2026 (second quarter and half year 2025/26)

CECONOMY is the German holding company behind MediaMarkt and Saturn, the largest consumer-electronics retail chain in Europe, with roughly 1,000 stores across 11 countries and about EUR 24 billion of annual sales. Since November 2025 it has been 85.2%-owned by JD.com, the Chinese e-commerce group, following a takeover offer whose acceptance window has closed.

---

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC

Across these three calls the story does not change — and that consistency is the single most striking feature of the file. Management tells the same story in the same words three times, with the numbers moving in the promised direction each time.

The spine of it is a claimed shift "from a classical retailer into what we call an omnichannel service platform" (December 2025), repeated almost verbatim in February and May. The proof points are always the same four: consecutive quarters of profitability growth (11 in December, 12 in February), a rising Net Promoter Score (a customer-recommendation gauge: 61, then 61, then 62), a rising online share of sales (30% at its peak in the first quarter), and a rising contribution from what management calls "growth businesses" — retail media (selling advertising space to suppliers), services and solutions, a third-party marketplace, private label, and renting out floor space.

What genuinely expands over the three calls is that last item, and it expands with numbers rather than adjectives. Growth businesses went from 31% of gross profit in fiscal 2022/23 to 33%, then 36% (December 2025), then "approximately 40% of our gross profit, up from 35% a year ago" (May 2026). By February this was "already a EUR 1 billion business" on a full-year basis. That is the one part of the narrative that is doing real work.

What quietly contracts is Germany. In December the domestic market is barely discussed. By February it is "softer demand in Germany and Austria." By May it is "demand in Germany and Austria remains somewhat subdued, but we are managing that actively," with an admission that the region "started Q1 slightly below expectation from an EBIT perspective, mainly driven by top line." The remedy offered is narrower each time — by May it has shrunk to "extreme focus on the top 200" products, which management says are 40% of sales. A retailer that has retreated to defending 200 stock-keeping units out of 15,000 online is not describing a strong home market.

What is introduced and never developed is JD.com. Every call carries a JD section; none of them contains a number, a synergy target, or a named initiative. In December it is "significant experience, especially in logistics and technology." In February, asked directly whether the Joybuy Express delivery service is coming to MediaMarkt, the chief executive answers "it is too early to comment on specific services." In May the question is only about approval timing. Three calls, three deflections. Whatever value JD brings, management has not quantified one euro of it in public.

Finally, the leadership changed mid-story. Kai-Ulrich Deissner opened the May call by noting it was "my 14th, but also my last earnings call" and introduced the chief financial officer, Remko Rijnders, as "my soon-to-be successor." A chief-financial-officer-to-chief-executive handover, executed while a controlling shareholder waits on regulatory clearance, is a continuity choice, not a change of direction.

---

## 2. CLAIMS vs FINANCIALS (forensic)

This is where the file breaks in two. The operating claims hold up well. The claims a shareholder actually gets paid on do not.

Nine-month reported operating profit is about EUR 161 million and nine-month net income swung to positive EUR 23 million from negative EUR 4 million a year earlier. | Holds — on the adjusted measure |
| Sales growing | All three calls | The June-2026 quarter delivered EUR 5,273 million against EUR 4,803 million a year earlier, up 9.8% — the fastest growth in the series. Nine-month sales EUR 18,345 million, up 4.1%. | Holds, and better than guided |

Reported net income was negative EUR 39 million in 2023, positive EUR 76 million in 2024, negative EUR 35 million in 2025. Trailing-twelve-month diluted earnings per share is negative EUR 0.03. Return on invested capital is 1.8%. Five straight years in which the company earned essentially nothing for its owners. | **Diverges** |

What is causing the EBIT to be negative is the investment that we did in our future" | Dec 2025 | This is the central forensic issue. In 2024/25, adjusted operating profit of EUR 378 million sat on top of a *negative* reported operating result. **The single sentence that matters:** the screener flags this name at 2.9 times free cash flow.
