The market is not looking the wrong way here. Our own screen was.

The usual shape of a disagreement in this book is that the street prices terminal decline into a business with stable or growing earnings power. That is not the situation. The street prices CECONOMY at 4.39 times enterprise value to operating cash profit and prices Currys plc, the same business model in a neighbouring market, at 4.55 times, both checked live on 31 August 2026. The market has looked at two European box retailers and given them the same number. That is a considered judgement, not neglect.

Where we do disagree is with our own inputs, and the correction cuts against the position rather than for it. Three assumptions embedded in the screening record are wrong.

First, the price-to-free-cash-flow multiple of 2.9 times and the trailing free cash flow of EUR 731 million. Under current lease accounting, store rent is removed from operating cash flow and reappears in financing; those payments totalled about EUR 524 million over the last four quarters. Free cash flow to the equity is therefore about EUR 207 million and the multiple is about 9.6 times. Management guides to the corrected number in public: on 17 December 2025 the chief financial officer reaffirmed 'a stable cash flow of EUR 200 million per year'. The company has been telling anyone who listens what the real figure is.

Second, the discounted-cash-flow fair value of EUR 19.6 carried on the stock page, and the associated margin-of-safety readings of plus 79% on discounted cash flow, plus 76% on owner earnings and plus 58% on earnings power. All four are computed off the uncorrected cash-flow figure and are therefore inflated by roughly three and a half times at the input. A fair value five times the traded price for a retailer earning 1.8% on invested capital should have been rejected on sight. Notably, the two methods that read minus 100%, the Graham and the fifteen-times-intrinsic screens, are the ones anchored to reported earnings, and reported earnings are approximately zero. The disagreement between our own methods was the signal.

Third, the implied claim on EUR 4.60. It does not exist. JD.com's offer window closed on 10 November 2025 and the shares trade 13.6% below that price for the good reason that no holder can collect it.

Where we do hold a modest non-consensus view, it is on the business rather than the security, and it is not enough to buy. The market appears to treat this as a structurally shrinking electronics retailer, and it is not one: sales grew 9.8% in the quarter to 30 June 2026, the growth businesses moved from 31% to about 40% of gross profit in three years, and retail-media income nearly doubled in the half year to March 2026. Retail media in particular monetises store traffic and first-party customer data that a pure online competitor cannot reach. That argues the business is worth roughly EUR 4.45 a share rather than EUR 3.975. It is a 12% disagreement, not an investable one.

One street assumption we would flag as genuinely unexamined, because nobody asked it on any of the three calls in the file: what a minority holder is entitled to receive. No analyst asked what price a delisting purchase offer would be struck at, or whether a domination agreement is contemplated. The absence of that question is the clearest evidence that the remaining float is not being underwritten by anybody.
forcing_function:
There are two candidate forcing functions and, honestly assessed, neither delivers the money to a holder buying today.

The first is dated and hard, and it belongs to somebody else. On the 13 May 2026 call the chief executive named 10 November 2026 as the long-stop date for the JD.com transaction, saying completion was expected 'in the second half of the calendar year, but obviously before November 10, which is the long stop date'. That date is binding on JD and CECONOMY. It is not a payment to a minority shareholder. Completion transfers control that JD already exercises at 85.2%; outside holders receive nothing on that day.

The second is the one that would actually pay, and it is neither dated nor promised. German law gives a controlling shareholder three routes past a minority. At 95% it can compel a buy-out; JD is at 85.2%, nearly five percentage points short, and would have to buy roughly 23 million shares in the market to get there, which in a stock trading 6,252 shares a day is not a quiet operation. Above 75%, which JD cleared long ago, it may put a domination and profit-transfer agreement to a shareholder meeting; that obliges it to offer minorities an annual guaranteed payment and a cash exit valued on the company's intrinsic worth, reviewable by a court in appraisal proceedings that historically settle above the offered figure. That is the genuinely asymmetric outcome for a holder here. And a delisting purchase offer would be struck at the trailing six-month volume-weighted average price, which we estimate at roughly EUR 4.05 today, about 2% above the current quote.

Management's own words on the timing of the third route are the best evidence available and they are deliberately vague: a delisting 'between 3 and 6 months after closing', immediately qualified with 'that's part of, not 100% easy process. So I can't give you a precise timing.' No domination agreement has been announced. No accumulation toward 95% has been disclosed to us.

The operating forcing function is real but small: the fiscal year ends 30 September 2026, when the EUR 500 million adjusted operating profit target and all nine key performance indicators from the 2023 capital-markets day come due, with results due around December 2026. A clean delivery would validate the mix shift. But the market has already told us how much it cares. The 9 July 2026 strategy day, at which management said the next phase would be set out and that 'we don't believe that EUR 500 million is the ceiling', moved the shares to EUR 4.20 on 147,766 units and was fully given back the following session at EUR 3.88. When the plan presentation round-trips in a day, the operating story is not what is holding the price.

The honest summary: the only event that re-rates this security is a decision by JD.com to pay for the rest of the company, and JD has no obligation to make it, no announced intention to make it, and a direct economic interest in the share price staying low until it does.
valley_of_death:
There is no cash-burn hump and no maturity wall here. The risks over the next three to nine months are the ordinary kind, plus one structural trap that is specific to this security.

Solvency is not the concern. At 30 June 2026 the company held EUR 1,091 million of cash against EUR 2,597 million of total debt, of which roughly EUR 1.7 billion is capitalised store rent rather than borrowing; on a pre-lease basis it sits close to net cash. Suppliers finance the working capital, with a cash conversion cycle of negative 34 days, and capital spending is trivial at about EUR 33 million a quarter against EUR 168 million of depreciation. The financial-strength score of 2.3 on the standard bankruptcy screen looks alarming and is a false reading for a negative-working-capital retailer.

What can go wrong, in order of likelihood.

The first is the seasonal cash swing, which is violent and will be misread. Net debt was nil at 31 December 2025, EUR 1,596 million at 31 March 2026 and EUR 1,506 million at 30 June 2026. The March quarter alone showed a EUR 1,483 million cash outflow as the Christmas payables unwound. Anyone marking this position on a quarterly balance sheet without adjusting for the cycle will see leverage appearing and disappearing that is not real.

The second is the fiscal year ending 30 September 2026, which is the moment the three-year plan comes due. Management set a EUR 500 million adjusted operating profit target at the 2023 capital-markets day and has repeated it 'precisely to the last decimal since'. Nine of nine key indicators fall due on that date. Two things could disappoint. The German and Austrian markets have been described as soft on both the February and May calls, with the region starting the year 'slightly below expectation from an EBIT perspective, mainly driven by top line', and Germany is roughly a third of the business. And the target is measured on the adjusted figure; the reported figure has run about EUR 300 million lower every year for three years, so hitting the target and reporting another near-zero net profit are entirely compatible outcomes.

The third is the regulatory tail on the JD transaction, which the current market regime says to take more seriously than usual. As of 13 May 2026 foreign-investment approvals were still outstanding in Austria, Germany and Spain, and the European foreign-subsidies review in Brussels was described only as constructive discussions. The regime read of 18 August 2026 is explicit that clearance-based deal-risk models are now mis-specified: Paramount's transaction satisfied every regulatory condition and cleared 68 countries and is frozen regardless, to a 2027 trial. A Chinese buyer of European retail infrastructure and customer data faces exactly the kind of political review that does not resolve on a schedule. The 10 November 2026 long-stop date falls inside the nine-month window.

The fourth, and the one that has no natural end, is that nothing happens. There is no dividend. The shares have de-rated from EUR 4.49 on 20 March 2026 to EUR 3.975, drifting down through a summer in which the operating results improved. A holder waiting for a controlling shareholder to decide receives nothing for waiting.

The fifth is liquidity itself. On 31 August 2026 the shares traded 6,252 units, roughly EUR 25,000 for a session. In an adverse tape, this is a security in which the exit is priced, not offered.
positioning_washout:
The forced selling has already happened, which is precisely why there is no washout left to buy.

The shareholder base was reshaped in one move. JD.com's tender took it to 85.2% by the end of November 2025, and every institution that wanted the offer price took it. What remains is a 14.8% float of roughly 72 million shares, worth about EUR 285 million. On 31 August 2026 that float turned over 6,252 shares.

There is a visible second wave in the tape, in late March 2026. The shares traded EUR 4.49 on 20 March and EUR 4.26 on 30 March on 436,130 shares, the heaviest session in the six months of data reviewed, and never recovered the level. Volume of that shape in a stock of this float, ending in a permanent de-rate, has the signature of index-tracking or mandate-driven liquidation following the float reduction. We do not have a source naming the cause and will not assert one, but the flow is real and it is behind us, not ahead of us.

The mechanical selling that could still come is smaller and slower. There is no dividend to cut, so there is no income-mandate exodus to trigger. What remains is the residual passive and small-cap ownership that a formal delisting would eventually force out. That is a real seller, but it would arrive only after a delisting application, which management said on 13 May 2026 would come 'between 3 and 6 months after closing' with no precise timing, and which would itself be accompanied by a statutory purchase offer at the trailing six-month average price. In other words, the last forced sellers get an exit at roughly the current price, which is a floor for them and a ceiling for anyone buying today hoping to sell into their panic.

The more useful reading of positioning here is the reverse of the usual one. The market regime read of 18 August 2026 flags the tape as complacent-long, with fund-manager cash at 3.5% and equity overweights the highest since November 2021, and counsels smaller adds and wider entry discounts. This name offers no entry discount and is illiquid enough that a position could not be reduced quickly if the regime turned. The 200-day average of EUR 4.198 sitting above the 50-day average of EUR 3.939 confirms the trend is down, not washed out.

One genuine mechanical event is worth watching for the record: the share count. The weighted diluted count was 502.8 million in the December-2025 quarter against 485.2 million basic, implying a convertible instrument that would dilute existing holders by roughly 3.6% if it converts. That is small, but in a stub with no float it is a real overhang.
moderator_conclusion:
Pass for now, and the reason is worth stating plainly because it is a correction to our own input rather than a judgement about the company.

CECONOMY is a better business than its reputation and a worse security than its screen. On the business: sales in the quarter to 30 June 2026 were EUR 5,273 million, up 9.8% year on year and the fastest growth in the series, with the net loss narrowing to EUR 66 million from EUR 114 million and nine-month net income turning positive. Management has grown adjusted operating profit for twelve consecutive quarters, publishes a nine-item scorecard it can visibly fail, and has moved the higher-margin part of the business, retail media, marketplace, services, private label and rented space, from 31% of gross profit three years ago to about 40%. Retail media is a genuine asset: it monetises store traffic and customer data that no pure online rival can reach. This is not a melting ice cube, and the reflexive short case is wrong.

On the security, three things disqualify it at any meaningful size.

The first is that the cheapness is an accounting artifact. The screen reads 2.9 times free cash flow on EUR 731 million. Under current lease accounting, store rent leaves operating cash flow and reappears in financing; those payments were about EUR 524 million over the last four quarters. Corrected, free cash flow to the equity is about EUR 207 million and the multiple is about 9.6 times. Management guides to the corrected number in public, reaffirming on 17 December 2025 'a stable cash flow of EUR 200 million per year'. The same error inflates the EUR 19.6 fair value on the stock page by roughly three and a half times at the input.

The second is that there is no discount to a peer. Checked live today, CECONOMY trades at 4.39 times enterprise value to operating cash profit against Currys plc at 4.55 times, the same model in a neighbouring market. Best Buy's 7.46 times is earned: it returns 17.2% on invested capital, CECONOMY 1.8%. Reconciling the parts with what the equity actually earns after roughly EUR 252 million of annual interest gives a base fair value of EUR 4.45, about 12% above the EUR 3.975 quote, against an adverse case of EUR 2.95. Half a euro of upside against a full euro of downside is not a position.

The third, and the one that would keep this out even at a better price, is the structure. JD.com holds 85.2%, above the 75% that permits a domination agreement and below the 95% that permits a compulsory buy-out, which is the one position that gives it every option and the minority none. The acceptance window on its EUR 4.60 offer closed on 10 November 2025; nothing bought today has a claim on it. Any statutory delisting purchase offer would be priced off a trailing six-month average, roughly EUR 4.05 now and falling as the price falls. That is a mirror, not a floor, which is why no structural downside floor is recorded here. And the controlling shareholder's economic interest is served by a low price for as long as the exit is undecided. The free float is 14.8% and traded EUR 25,000 of value on 31 August 2026.

On the catalyst, applying this book's neutrality rule: the status is recorded as could not be verified, and that has moved the conviction neither up nor down. Our newest verifiable material is the 13 May 2026 call, on which management pushed completion from the first half of 2026 to the second half and named 10 November 2026 as the long-stop date. The window that guidance points at opened after that call, and no dated source covering it could be obtained in this session. What matters for the score is what was judged on its own merits: a fairly valued, low-return franchise with a real mix shift, poor risk and reward, and a minority position on the wrong side of its controlling holder.

The regime read of 18 August 2026 reinforces the call rather than driving it. Merger arbitrage is the demoted lane, and specifically because the tail got worse: state and political review now freezes deals that have cleared every regulator, which is the exact shape of the risk facing a Chinese acquirer awaiting a European foreign-subsidies decision and three national foreign-investment approvals. The instruction is to underwrite the legal event, never the spread. Here there is not even a spread to underwrite. The tape is also complacent-long and counsels wider entry discounts and smaller adds; this name offers no discount and no liquidity in which to reduce.

What would change the call, and it is specific. A domination and profit-transfer agreement put to a shareholder meeting, or a disclosed accumulation toward the 95% buy-out threshold, would convert this from a stub into a court-reviewable claim on intrinsic value and would justify revisiting at once. So would the shares trading below about EUR 3.20, roughly 28% under our base fair value, where the adverse case is genuinely paid for. Absent either, we are declining to own the smallest, least liquid, least informed part of a capital structure controlled by someone whose interests run the other way.
sop_fair_value: EUR 4.45 a share (base case), against EUR 3.975 in the market on 31 August 2026. Adverse case EUR 2.95, favourable case EUR 5.60.
sop_breakdown:
Base case, built on estimated operating cash profit for the year to 30 September 2026 of about EUR 780 million (nine months actual EUR 651 million plus an estimated EUR 130 million final quarter), split into the two halves of the business management itself reports on.

Part one, Retail Core, the roughly 1,000 MediaMarkt and Saturn stores plus their online channel across 11 countries: about EUR 480 million of operating cash profit at 4.0 times, a modest discount to Currys plc at 4.55 times as checked live on 31 August 2026, because Currys earns 7.4% on invested capital against CECONOMY's 1.8% and reports positive net income. Contributes EUR 1,920 million of enterprise value.

Part two, the growth businesses, meaning retail media, services and solutions, the third-party marketplace, private label and rented floor space, which management put at about 40% of gross profit in the half year to March 2026 and about EUR 1 billion of annual income: about EUR 300 million of operating cash profit after allocating a share of the store, staff and logistics costs they consume, at 6.5 times. That is a 62% premium to the retail multiple, which the higher margins and the near-doubling of retail-media income justify, and a deep discount to any pure-play advertising or marketplace comparable, which is right because this business is captive to the store estate and has never been given a separate balance sheet. Contributes EUR 1,950 million.

Enterprise value EUR 3,870 million, a blended 4.96 times. Deduct net debt of EUR 1,506 million as at 30 June 2026 (total debt EUR 2,597 million less cash EUR 1,091 million). The definition used here is total net debt including lease liabilities, matching the definition under which the peer multiples are computed. Note that the March-2026 balance sheet showed EUR 1,678 million of that debt as capitalised store leases, so the input file's note describing capitalised leases as nil is inconsistent with the company's own prior-quarter statement; the two definitions must not be mixed, and the enterprise multiples above are consistently post-lease on both sides. Note also the seasonality: net debt was nil at 31 December 2025 and swings by more than EUR 1.5 billion through the year, so the 30 June figure used here is close to the seasonal peak and is the conservative choice. Equity value EUR 2,364 million across 485.2 million shares equals EUR 4.87 a share on the parts.

The parts figure is then averaged with an earnings check, because a third of the operating cash profit is paid away in interest and lease charges before an owner receives anything. Adjusted operating profit of about EUR 500 million less roughly EUR 252 million of annual interest, taxed at 35%, is about EUR 0.33 a share; at 12 times, a fair multiple for a low-growth retailer earning under 2% on capital, that is EUR 3.98. The average of EUR 4.87 and EUR 3.98 gives the base case of EUR 4.45.

Overlays considered and deliberately not credited: there is no pending distribution, no announced asset sale, and no live tender. The EUR 4.60 offer price is not an overlay, because its acceptance window closed on 10 November 2025 and no holder buying today acquires a claim on it. A statutory delisting purchase offer would be struck at the trailing six-month volume-weighted average price, which we estimate at roughly EUR 4.05 from the traded tape, only about 2% above the current quote and falling as the price falls; that is a moving mirror, not a floor, so no structural downside floor is recorded.
risk_reward: Poor, and it is the clearest number in the file. From EUR 3.975 the base case at EUR 4.45 is about EUR 0.48 a share of upside; the adverse case at EUR 2.95 is about EUR 1.03 a share of downside. peer_comps_note: Checked live on 31 August 2026, there is no relative discount to capture. CECONOMY trades at 4.39 times enterprise value to operating cash profit; Currys plc, its closest listed comparable and the same low-margin, high-volume electronics model, trades at 4.55 times. On sales the gap looks wider, 0.144 times against Currys' 0.253 times, but that gap is a margin difference rather than a valuation one: CECONOMY converts about 3.3% of sales into operating cash profit against Currys' 5.6%, so the two multiples describe the same enterprise value per unit of profit. Fnac Darty at 6.77 times is not a fair anchor upward; it is the more indebted comparable, at 4.7 times net debt to operating cash profit against CECONOMY's 1.9 times. One caveat on how to read any remaining gap: all three European names move on the same unresolved driver, the European consumer-electronics demand cycle, so a discount to Currys or Fnac Darty would be shared sector exposure rather than anything specific to this name. As it happens there is no such gap to argue over.
interrogator_dossier:
# CECONOMY AG (CEC.DE) — Forensic Interrogator Dossier
**Date of review:** 31 August 2026 · **Price used:** EUR 3.975 (XETRA close, 31 Aug 2026) · **Market value:** about EUR 1.93 billion
**Transcripts reviewed:** 17 December 2025 (full-year 2024/25), 11 February 2026 (first quarter 2025/26), 13 May 2026 (second quarter and half year 2025/26)

CECONOMY is the German holding company behind MediaMarkt and Saturn, the largest consumer-electronics retail chain in Europe, with roughly 1,000 stores across 11 countries and about EUR 24 billion of annual sales. Since November 2025 it has been 85.2%-owned by JD.com, the Chinese e-commerce group, following a takeover offer whose acceptance window has closed.

---

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC

Across these three calls the story does not change — and that consistency is the single most striking feature of the file. Management tells the same story in the same words three times, with the numbers moving in the promised direction each time.

The spine of it is a claimed shift "from a classical retailer into what we call an omnichannel service platform" (December 2025), repeated almost verbatim in February and May. The proof points are always the same four: consecutive quarters of profitability growth (11 in December, 12 in February), a rising Net Promoter Score (a customer-recommendation gauge: 61, then 61, then 62), a rising online share of sales (30% at its peak in the first quarter), and a rising contribution from what management calls "growth businesses" — retail media (selling advertising space to suppliers), services and solutions, a third-party marketplace, private label, and renting out floor space.

What genuinely expands over the three calls is that last item, and it expands with numbers rather than adjectives. Growth businesses went from 31% of gross profit in fiscal 2022/23 to 33%, then 36% (December 2025), then "approximately 40% of our gross profit, up from 35% a year ago" (May 2026). By February this was "already a EUR 1 billion business" on a full-year basis. That is the one part of the narrative that is doing real work.

What quietly contracts is Germany. In December the domestic market is barely discussed. By February it is "softer demand in Germany and Austria." By May it is "demand in Germany and Austria remains somewhat subdued, but we are managing that actively," with an admission that the region "started Q1 slightly below expectation from an EBIT perspective, mainly driven by top line." The remedy offered is narrower each time — by May it has shrunk to "extreme focus on the top 200" products, which management says are 40% of sales. A retailer that has retreated to defending 200 stock-keeping units out of 15,000 online is not describing a strong home market.

What is introduced and never developed is JD.com. Every call carries a JD section; none of them contains a number, a synergy target, or a named initiative. In December it is "significant experience, especially in logistics and technology." In February, asked directly whether the Joybuy Express delivery service is coming to MediaMarkt, the chief executive answers "it is too early to comment on specific services." In May the question is only about approval timing. Three calls, three deflections. Whatever value JD brings, management has not quantified one euro of it in public.

Finally, the leadership changed mid-story. Kai-Ulrich Deissner opened the May call by noting it was "my 14th, but also my last earnings call" and introduced the chief financial officer, Remko Rijnders, as "my soon-to-be successor." A chief-financial-officer-to-chief-executive handover, executed while a controlling shareholder waits on regulatory clearance, is a continuity choice, not a change of direction.

---

## 2. CLAIMS vs FINANCIALS (forensic)

This is where the file breaks in two. The operating claims hold up well. The claims a shareholder actually gets paid on do not.

| Management claim | Where | What the numbers show | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| "12 quarters in a row" of profitability growth; adjusted operating profit around EUR 500 million for 2025/26 | Feb 2026, reaffirmed May 2026 | The seasonal shape they described is being met: the December quarter delivered EUR 311 million of adjusted operating profit, which they said is 64% of the full-year budget. Nine-month reported operating profit is about EUR 161 million and nine-month net income swung to positive EUR 23 million from negative EUR 4 million a year earlier. | Holds — on the adjusted measure |
| Sales growing | All three calls | The June-2026 quarter delivered EUR 5,273 million against EUR 4,803 million a year earlier, up 9.8% — the fastest growth in the series. Nine-month sales EUR 18,345 million, up 4.1%. | Holds, and better than guided |
| The turnaround is reaching the bottom line | Implied throughout | It is not. Reported net income was negative EUR 39 million in 2023, positive EUR 76 million in 2024, negative EUR 35 million in 2025. Trailing-twelve-month diluted earnings per share is negative EUR 0.03. Return on invested capital is 1.8%. Five straight years in which the company earned essentially nothing for its owners. | **Diverges** |
| "Adjusted EBIT indeed improved to a staggering amount of EUR 378 million. What is causing the EBIT to be negative is the investment that we did in our future" | Dec 2025 | This is the central forensic issue. In 2024/25, adjusted operating profit of EUR 378 million sat on top of a *negative* reported operating result. In 2025/26 the adjusted figure is guided to about EUR 500 million while reported operating profit tracks toward roughly EUR 200 million. A roughly EUR 300 million annual gap, attributed each year to a different one-off — JD transaction costs, Poland restructuring, German store restructuring, German severance. **An add-back that recurs every year for three years is a cost, not an adjustment.** | **Diverges — the most important divergence in the file** |
| "We increased free cash flow by 180%, now reaching EUR 337 million" | Dec 2025 | Directionally true on the company's own definition, and the screener's trailing-twelve-month figure of EUR 731 million looks spectacular. Both overstate what an owner receives. Under current lease accounting, store rent is stripped out of operating cash flow and reappears in financing: those payments ran about EUR 524 million across the last four quarters. Net of them, true free cash flow to the equity is roughly **EUR 207 million**. | **Diverges — the headline cheapness is an artifact** |
| "We expect a stable cash flow of EUR 200 million per year, and we're also not changing that number" | Dec 2025 | Management's own target corroborates the corrected figure almost exactly. They are guiding to EUR 200 million; the corrected trailing number is EUR 207 million. The company is telling you the true number while the screening screen reads EUR 731 million. | Holds — and it is the honest number |
| The mix shift to higher-margin growth businesses is lifting profitability | May 2026 | Partly. In the seasonally dominant December quarter, gross profit was EUR 1,147 million on EUR 7,606 million of sales — a 15.08% gross margin against 16.92% a year earlier, a fall of 184 basis points in the quarter that carries roughly two-thirds of annual profit. Management never mentioned it. Operating profit still rose, because costs fell faster. | **Diverges — a real deterioration went unremarked** |
| Deleveraging / balance-sheet strength | Implied ("focus on cost, liquidity and profitability", May 2026) | At 30 June 2026: cash EUR 1,091 million against total debt EUR 2,597 million, so net debt EUR 1,506 million. The March-2026 balance sheet shows EUR 1,678 million of that debt is capitalised store leases, so on a pre-lease basis the company is close to net-cash. Interest expense nonetheless runs about EUR 252 million a year, which consumes half of the guided adjusted operating profit. | Mixed — solvency fine, but interest is a real claim |
| Dividend policy "15% to 25% of the net profit... still in place" | Dec 2025 | Technically true and practically empty. No dividend has been paid in any quarter in the data. A payout ratio applied to a net profit of approximately zero pays approximately zero. | Hollow |

**The single sentence that matters:** the screener flags this name at 2.9 times free cash flow. On management's own cash guidance of EUR 200 million a year, against a EUR 1.93 billion market value, the real multiple is closer to **9.6 times**. That is a fair price for a low-return retailer, not a deep-value one.

---

## 3. TONE & CONFIDENCE TRAJECTORY

**Rating: Stable-to-Rising on delivery, but the specificity is shrinking.**

- **December 2025 — confident and expansive.** "We had already shared some preliminary numbers with you back in October, but I'm sure you will see some very strong performance across the board today." The chief executive volunteers the eleven-quarter streak unprompted and calls the free-cash-flow number "a very hard measure."
- **February 2026 — the most assured of the three.** The peak-season quarter is framed as a test passed: "it's a stress test for us... the key message here today is we've delivered." The chief financial officer volunteers a quarter-by-quarter profit distribution (64% / 6% / 1% / 29%) that is unusually specific and lets outsiders check the guidance themselves. That is the behaviour of a team that expects to hit the number.
- **May 2026 — confident but valedictory, and noticeably more defensive on Germany.** "We must not get and we are not arrogant. We know there is still significant work ahead of us." The German answer is entirely cost-and-benchmark language: "a very strong cost program... focusing on location costs, but also a lot on indirect spend... really benchmarking the cost between the countries."

The offensive-to-defensive shift is regional rather than global: the international portfolio (Turkey, Spain, Hungary, Italy, Poland) is discussed in growth terms throughout, while the home market moves steadily into the efficiency vocabulary. Management is candid that this is happening — "this only shows how valuable our diversified international portfolio is" (February) — which is honest framing of a genuine weakness, but it is still a weakness in the market that carries the brand.

The one place confidence visibly narrows is targets. In December, asked to update the 2023 capital-markets-day free-cash-flow and margin targets, the chief financial officer answered: "we will not comment on numbers in any detail." Refusing to refresh a three-year-old target set while reaffirming only the single headline number from it is a narrowing of accountability, not an expression of confidence.

---

## 4. GUIDANCE CREDIBILITY

**Score: Medium-High on the adjusted operating measure. Low on anything below it.**

The track record on what they actually guide is good. In December 2025 they guided to "around EUR 500 million" of adjusted operating profit for 2025/26 and gave the seasonal shape. In February they delivered EUR 311 million in the first quarter — consistent with the 64% they said the quarter should carry — and reaffirmed. In May they reaffirmed again with the half year up EUR 43 million. Sales came in ahead of guidance in 2024/25: "sales reached EUR 23.1 billion... that's more than the moderate growth that we initially guided." The screener records a two-of-three quarterly beat rate. Nothing here looks like sandbagging; it looks like a modest, achievable number set once and hit.

Two things hold the score down.

First, **the guided measure is not the earned measure.** Management guides adjusted operating profit and reports against it faithfully, while the reported line — the one that feeds book value and cash taxes — comes in roughly EUR 300 million lower every year for reasons re-labelled each time. Guidance credibility is high *within a frame the company chose*, which is a weaker thing than it sounds.

Second, **the deal timetable has already slipped once, on the record.** In December 2025 the chief executive said closing was expected "for the first half of the next calendar year." In February he said "we remain very confident and expect to close in the first half of 2026." By 13 May the same executive said: "the closing date in the second half of the calendar year is what we're referring to... obviously before November 10, which is the long stop date." That is a six-month slip announced without being named as one. On the delisting that would follow, he was explicit that he could not commit: "between 3 and 6 months after closing, but that's part of — not 100% easy process. So I can't give you a precise timing."

---

## 5. ANALYST PRESSURE POINTS

Coverage of this name is thin and getting thinner, and the question list shows it — a mix of trade press, wire journalists, one small research house, and two hedge funds. The recurring pressure points:

- **Regulatory clearance for the JD transaction, asked in all three calls and never answered with substance.** In February, asked about the European foreign-subsidies review, the answer was "I cannot give you any color on this." In May, asked directly by Fred Ward of Verition Fund about Austrian approval timing and whether remedies would be required, the answer was: "these are very sensitive discussions, the confidentiality of which we respect 100%. So I cannot comment." **Two hedge funds asking approval-timing questions on consecutive calls is the tell that the pending clearance, not the operating business, is what the marginal buyer is trading.**
- **What JD actually brings.** Asked in February whether Joybuy Express would come to MediaMarkt: "too early to comment on specific services."
- **The gap between adjusted and reported profit.** A journalist asked this in December in the plainest possible terms — "your adjusted EBIT improved, but not your reported EBIT. Could you give a guidance for reported EBIT?" The answer explained the two add-backs and then guided only to the adjusted number. **No reported-profit guidance was given, then or since.** This is the most important unanswered question in the file, and only one person has asked it.
- **The stale capital-markets-day targets.** Ulrike Dauer of Dow Jones asked in December for updated free-cash-flow and margin targets. Declined.
- **German cost structure and store closures.** Asked in May; management said "at the moment, we don't" plan additional closures, immediately hedged with "we will always... look at the performance of our stores."
- **What comes after September 2026.** Asked in May whether there is meaningful profit upside beyond the EUR 500 million target, the answer was: "I cannot preempt what will be said in July about the next phase. But what I can preempt that we don't believe that EUR 500 million is the ceiling." The July strategy day has since happened; there is no transcript of it in this file, and the share price rose to EUR 4.20 on 9 July on 147,766 shares and gave the entire move back the following session at EUR 3.88. **The market's verdict on the new plan was a one-day round trip.**

**What analysts are not asking, and should be:** what a minority shareholder is actually entitled to receive. Nobody on any of these three calls asked what price a delisting purchase offer would be struck at, or whether JD intends a domination agreement or a buy-out of the remaining 14.8%. That silence is the single largest hole in the public discussion of this security.

## 6. RED FLAGS / GREEN FLAGS

**🔴 Red flags**

- 🔴 **The recurring "non-recurring" charge.** Roughly EUR 300 million a year separates adjusted from reported operating profit, three years running, each year for a different named reason (December 2025: JD transaction costs of EUR 32 million plus Poland restructuring; May 2026: German restructuring). Three consecutive years of exceptional items is a run rate.
- 🔴 **Peak-quarter gross margin fell 184 basis points** in the December 2025 quarter (15.08% against 16.92%), in the quarter carrying most of the year's profit, and was not mentioned on the February call — which instead led with an all-time-high online share and a record customer-satisfaction score.
- 🔴 **The free-cash-flow headline is an accounting artifact.** The trailing figure of EUR 731 million is roughly EUR 207 million once store-lease payments are counted. Management's own EUR 200 million target confirms the corrected number; the screening metric does not.
- 🔴 **The closing date slipped six months without being called a slip** (December 2025 and February 2026: first half of 2026 → 13 May 2026: second half, long stop 10 November).
- 🔴 **Liquidity has collapsed.** Free float is about 14.8% after JD's 85.2%. On 31 August 2026 the shares traded 6,252 units — roughly EUR 25,000 of turnover in a whole session. A position of any institutional size cannot be built or exited without moving the price.
- 🔴 **A dividend policy that pays nothing.** Reaffirmed in December 2025 as 15-25% of net profit; net profit is approximately zero and no dividend appears in the cash-flow statements.
- 🔴 **The controlling shareholder's interest is opposed to the minority's on price.** At 85.2%, JD controls the board, the guidance and the disclosure calendar, and any statutory delisting purchase offer would be struck off a trailing six-month average share price. Every euro the shares do not rise before that moment is a euro JD does not pay.

**🟢 Green flags**

- 🟢 **The June-2026 quarter was the best in the series:** sales EUR 5,273 million, up 9.8% year on year, with the net loss narrowing to EUR 66 million from EUR 114 million and operating cash flow of EUR 236 million.
- 🟢 **The mix shift is real and measured, not asserted:** growth businesses moved from 31% of gross profit in 2022/23 to about 40% in the half year to March 2026, with retail-media income "nearly doubled" and marketplace live across 98% of the footprint after the January Switzerland launch.
- 🟢 **Unusual disclosure discipline.** The nine-key-indicator table is presented every quarter against a fixed September-2026 deadline, and three of the nine were hit early (December 2025). Publishing a scorecard you can visibly fail is a governance positive.
- 🟢 **The chief financial officer volunteered the quarterly profit distribution** (64/6/1/29) in February — a genuinely checkable disclosure that most managements withhold.
- 🟢 **Poland was fixed on the record, with a named mechanism**: new chief executive and chief financial officer, a matrix reporting structure, marketplace launch — and profit improved in consecutive quarters (February and May).
- 🟢 **Inventory discipline improved** to 8.8 weeks of stock reach (December 2025), and the cash conversion cycle is negative 34 days: suppliers fund the working capital.
- 🟢 **Balance-sheet solvency is not the issue.** Almost all of the EUR 1.5 billion of net debt is capitalised store rent; pre-lease, the company sits close to net cash.

---

## 7. HIDDEN SIGNALS

**The vocabulary migrated from "customers" to "cost" in exactly one region.** Turkey, Spain, Hungary, Italy and Poland are always described with growth verbs. Germany and Austria, from February onward, are described only with cost verbs — "location costs," "indirect spend," "benchmarking the cost between the countries," "on par with the benchmark of our company." Management never says the German business is in trouble; the word choice says it for them.

**"Brand equity" arrived as a defensive prop.** Asked in December whether Saturn survives, the chief executive answered by citing Brand Finance: brand value up EUR 500 million year over year to EUR 2.5 billion. Reaching for a third-party brand valuation to answer a store-format question is a tell that the format question is live, notwithstanding the flat denial that followed ("we have 2 options. It's MediaMarkt and it's Saturn. And it stays like that").

**The competition is never named.** Across three full calls there is not one mention of Amazon, Apple's direct channel, or any specific competitor. The environment is described only in the abstract — "highly competitive and volatile." A retailer whose category has been reshaped by a single online competitor for fifteen years and never says its name is managing the narrative.

**"Refurbished" is doing quiet double duty.** Sales "nearly tripled" (December) then grew "almost 400%" (February), presented as sustainability and customer choice. It is also, straightforwardly, a trade-down signal: customers reaching for cheaper goods. Management books it as a strategic win.

**The successor's voice is already the dominant one.** By May, Remko Rijnders is answering the German cost question, the Poland question and the margin question — the three hardest on the call — while the outgoing chief executive handles JD and the farewell. The handover was functionally complete before it was formally announced, and the incoming voice is a cost-and-benchmark voice, not a growth voice.

**Loyalty membership grew faster than plausible retail engagement.** 53 million members in December, 57 million by February — 4 million added in one quarter against a footprint of 11 countries. Management attributes this partly to merging the MediaMarkt and Saturn programmes in Germany. A merged-programme headcount and an engaged-customer headcount are not the same number, and only the first one is disclosed.

---

## 8. CAPITAL-ALLOCATION VERDICT (for the director)

**Classification: PIVOTING.**

The business is genuinely being rebuilt — a box retailer converting roughly 40% of its gross profit into advertising, marketplace, services and space rental, with twelve consecutive quarters of adjusted operating-profit growth and an accelerating top line (up 9.8% in the June-2026 quarter). That is not a dying company, and the reflexive "consumer electronics retail is finished" reading is wrong. But it is also not yet a strengthening one: reported net income has been approximately zero for five straight years, return on invested capital is 1.8%, and the peak-quarter gross margin fell 184 basis points in the most recent Christmas trading period. The pivot is real, incomplete, and running alongside a change of chief executive and a change of ownership.

**The single most important thing the director must weigh before sizing a position:**

> **This is a 14.8% minority stub in a company controlled by a shareholder whose economic interest is in a low share price, and the security's headline cheapness is an accounting artifact.**

Unpack both halves, because each is independently disqualifying at size.

On the *security*: JD.com holds 85.2%. The acceptance window on its EUR 4.60 offer has closed. A share bought today at EUR 3.975 carries no contractual claim on EUR 4.60 — it never will again. The German thresholds that matter are 95% (which would permit a compulsory buy-out of minorities) and 75% (already cleared, permitting a domination agreement with a court-reviewable cash exit). JD sits between them, in the one position that gives it every option and gives the minority none. If a delisting purchase offer comes, German law sets its floor at the trailing six-month volume-weighted average price — currently around EUR 4.05, or about 2% above today's quote, and a figure that falls as the share price falls. That is not a floor; it is a mirror. Meanwhile the shares traded EUR 25,000 of value on 31 August 2026.

On the *cheapness*: the screen reads 2.9 times free cash flow. Strip out the lease payments that current accounting routes through financing, and free cash flow to the equity is about EUR 207 million — which is what management itself guides to ("a stable cash flow of EUR 200 million per year," December 2025). That is 9.6 times, on a business earning a 1.8% return on invested capital. On enterprise value to operating cash profit, the stock trades at 4.4 times against Currys plc — its closest listed comparable, checked live on 31 August 2026 — at 4.55 times. **There is no discount to the peer group. The cheap headline was measuring the wrong thing.**

Size, if at all, as a small special-situation stub with the exit risk understood — never as a value position.

### Economic moat and terminal-value assessment

**Moat type: intangible brand plus scale-cost, and it is narrow.** MediaMarkt and Saturn hold leading share in most of their 11 markets, and the brand carries an independently measured EUR 2.5 billion of equity (Brand Finance, cited December 2025). Scale buys purchasing terms and funds a logistics network — 16 regional fulfilment centres, 10 of 14 planned German hubs live — that a subscale rival cannot replicate. Fifty-seven million loyalty members and a 37% in-store pickup rate on online orders describe a real omnichannel position that pure e-commerce cannot match on large appliances, installation and after-sales service.

**But width is judged on returns, and the returns are thin.** Return on invested capital is 1.8%. Return on equity flatters at 10.6% only because the equity base has shrunk (book value per share has compounded down 15.7% a year over five years). Net margin is negative 0.2%. The comparison that settles it: Best Buy, the same business model in a healthier market, earns a 17.2% return on invested capital and trades at 7.5 times enterprise value to operating cash profit; CECONOMY earns 1.8% and trades at 4.4 times. **The multiple gap is earned, not a mispricing.** A moat that cannot cover its cost of capital is narrow by definition.

**Moat trend: stable, on balance, with one genuine warning.** Cutting for erosion: the 184-basis-point peak-quarter gross-margin decline, a soft home market, and refurbished-goods growth that signals customer trade-down. Cutting the other way, and doing so with measured evidence: the growth businesses moved from 31% to about 40% of gross profit in three years, and those revenue lines — advertising, marketplace commission, service attachment, space rental — carry structurally higher margins and are less exposed to the electronics replacement cycle. Retail media in particular is a genuine widening asset: it monetises store traffic and first-party customer data that Amazon cannot access. The two forces roughly cancel.

**Secular threat: material, not terminal.** The relevant structural force is retail channel shift — the migration of consumer-electronics purchasing to Amazon and to manufacturers' direct channels. It is a real and permanent compressor of the core box business, and management's refusal to name a single competitor across three calls is not reassuring. But three pieces of evidence argue against terminal impairment: the company's own online share reached 30% and is growing 7-8% a year, so it is participating in the shift rather than being bypassed; large appliances, installation and repair retain a physical-service requirement that shows up in the hub rollout and the 37% pickup rate; and the peer set is not collapsing — Currys has risen from 106p to 152p over the past year. Physical electronics retail in Europe is a shrinking-margin, low-return business, not a disappearing one.

**Is the cheapness a fear print or a value trap? Neither — it is a measurement error.** Once free cash flow is corrected for lease payments and the multiple is set against its live peer, the stock is not cheap. There is no discount to explain away. What remains is a fairly priced, low-return retailer executing a credible mix shift, wrapped in a minority-stub structure that hands the pricing power to the majority holder.

Management credibility 3 of 5 · trajectory turning · a narrow but real moat · moat trend steady · structural threat material.

bull_thesis:
The bull case is that this is a genuinely improving European retailer being valued as a dying one, and that a controlling shareholder eventually has to pay to take out the 14.8% it does not own.

Start with the operating evidence, because it is stronger than the reputation. CECONOMY runs MediaMarkt and Saturn, roughly 1,000 consumer-electronics stores across 11 countries and about EUR 24 billion of annual sales. Management has now delivered twelve consecutive quarters of growth in adjusted operating profit, and the growth is accelerating rather than fading: the quarter to 30 June 2026 produced sales of EUR 5,273 million against EUR 4,803 million a year earlier, up 9.8% and the fastest rate in the series, with the net loss narrowing to EUR 66 million from EUR 114 million. Full-year guidance of around EUR 500 million of adjusted operating profit was reaffirmed on 13 May 2026, and the December-2025 quarter delivered EUR 311 million of it, matching the 64% seasonal share the chief financial officer said that quarter should carry.

The substantive change underneath is a mix shift that management measures rather than asserts. What they call growth businesses, meaning retail media (selling advertising to suppliers against store traffic and customer data), services and solutions, a third-party marketplace, private label and rented floor space, moved from 31% of gross profit in fiscal 2022/23 to about 40% in the half year to March 2026, with retail-media income nearly doubling and the marketplace live across 98% of the footprint after the January 2026 Switzerland launch. Online is 30% of sales at its peak and growing 7-8% a year, and 37% of online orders are collected in a store, so the company is participating in the channel shift rather than being bypassed by it.

It is below the 95% at which minorities can simply be bought out. A holder at EUR 3.975 therefore owns a claim on whatever process JD eventually chooses, in a company a strategic buyer valued at EUR 4.60 a share in July 2025. On a parts basis the enterprise is worth about EUR 4.7 billion in the favourable case, roughly EUR 6.50 a share after debt.

The conditions this requires: the EUR 500 million adjusted operating target is delivered on 30 September 2026 and the roughly EUR 300 million of annual charges below it finally stops recurring; German demand stabilises; the pending European and national approvals clear so JD closes; and JD then chooses a route that pays minorities rather than leaving a stub outstanding indefinitely.
bear_thesis:
The bear case is not that the business fails. It is that the security is mismeasured, fairly priced, and structurally on the wrong side of its controlling shareholder.

The measurement error comes first, because it is what put this name on the screen. The screening record reads a price-to-free-cash-flow multiple of 2.9 times and a trailing free cash flow of EUR 731 million. Under current lease accounting, store rent is stripped out of operating cash flow and reappears in financing: those payments ran about EUR 524 million across the last four quarters. Net of them, free cash flow available to the equity is roughly EUR 207 million, which is 9.6 times the EUR 1.93 billion market value, not 2.9 times. The company is telling you the real figure while the screen reads three and a half times it.

The second problem is that the profit being celebrated is not the profit being earned. In 2024/25 an adjusted operating profit of EUR 378 million sat on top of a negative reported operating result. In 2025/26 the adjusted figure is guided to around EUR 500 million while reported operating profit is tracking toward roughly EUR 200 million. That is a gap of about EUR 300 million a year, three years running, attributed each year to a different named one-off: JD transaction costs of EUR 32 million and Polish restructuring in December 2025, German restructuring in May 2026. An add-back that appears every year is a cost. The reported record is unambiguous: net income of negative EUR 39 million in 2023, positive EUR 76 million in 2024, negative EUR 35 million in 2025, and trailing diluted earnings per share of negative EUR 0.03. consensus_delta:
The market is not looking the wrong way here. Our own screen was.

The usual shape of a disagreement in this book is that the street prices terminal decline into a business with stable or growing earnings power. That is not the situation. The street prices CECONOMY at 4.39 times enterprise value to operating cash profit and prices Currys plc, the same business model in a neighbouring market, at 4.55 times, both checked live on 31 August 2026. The market has looked at two European box retailers and given them the same number. That is a considered judgement, not neglect.

Where we do disagree is with our own inputs, and the correction cuts against the position rather than for it. Three assumptions embedded in the screening record are wrong.

First, the price-to-free-cash-flow multiple of 2.9 times and the trailing free cash flow of EUR 731 million. Under current lease accounting, store rent is removed from operating cash flow and reappears in financing; those payments totalled about EUR 524 million over the last four quarters. Free cash flow to the equity is therefore about EUR 207 million and the multiple is about 9.6 times. Management guides to the corrected number in public: on 17 December 2025 the chief financial officer reaffirmed 'a stable cash flow of EUR 200 million per year'. The company has been telling anyone who listens what the real figure is.

Second, the discounted-cash-flow fair value of EUR 19.6 carried on the stock page, and the associated margin-of-safety readings of plus 79% on discounted cash flow, plus 76% on owner earnings and plus 58% on earnings power. All four are computed off the uncorrected cash-flow figure and are therefore inflated by roughly three and a half times at the input. A fair value five times the traded price for a retailer earning 1.8% on invested capital should have been rejected on sight. Notably, the two methods that read minus 100%, the Graham and the fifteen-times-intrinsic screens, are the ones anchored to reported earnings, and reported earnings are approximately zero. The disagreement between our own methods was the signal.

Third, the implied claim on EUR 4.60. It does not exist. JD.com's offer window closed on 10 November 2025 and the shares trade 13.6% below that price for the good reason that no holder can collect it.

Where we do hold a modest non-consensus view, it is on the business rather than the security, and it is not enough to buy. The market appears to treat this as a structurally shrinking electronics retailer, and it is not one: sales grew 9.8% in the quarter to 30 June 2026, the growth businesses moved from 31% to about 40% of gross profit in three years, and retail-media income nearly doubled in the half year to March 2026. No analyst asked what price a delisting purchase offer would be struck at, or whether a domination agreement is contemplated. forcing_function:
There are two candidate forcing functions and, honestly assessed, neither delivers the money to a holder buying today.

The first is dated and hard, and it belongs to somebody else. On the 13 May 2026 call the chief executive named 10 November 2026 as the long-stop date for the JD.com transaction, saying completion was expected 'in the second half of the calendar year, but obviously before November 10, which is the long stop date'. That date is binding on JD and CECONOMY. It is not a payment to a minority shareholder. Completion transfers control that JD already exercises at 85.2%; outside holders receive nothing on that day.

The second is the one that would actually pay, and it is neither dated nor promised. German law gives a controlling shareholder three routes past a minority. At 95% it can compel a buy-out; JD is at 85.2%, nearly five percentage points short, and would have to buy roughly 23 million shares in the market to get there, which in a stock trading 6,252 shares a day is not a quiet operation. Above 75%, which JD cleared long ago, it may put a domination and profit-transfer agreement to a shareholder meeting; that obliges it to offer minorities an annual guaranteed payment and a cash exit valued on the company's intrinsic worth, reviewable by a court in appraisal proceedings that historically settle above the offered figure. That is the genuinely asymmetric outcome for a holder here. And a delisting purchase offer would be struck at the trailing six-month volume-weighted average price, which we estimate at roughly EUR 4.05 today, about 2% above the current quote.

Management's own words on the timing of the third route are the best evidence available and they are deliberately vague: a delisting 'between 3 and 6 months after closing', immediately qualified with 'that's part of, not 100% easy process. So I can't give you a precise timing.' No domination agreement has been announced. No accumulation toward 95% has been disclosed to us.

The operating forcing function is real but small: the fiscal year ends 30 September 2026, when the EUR 500 million adjusted operating profit target and all nine key performance indicators from the 2023 capital-markets day come due, with results due around December 2026. A clean delivery would validate the mix shift. But the market has already told us how much it cares. The 9 July 2026 strategy day, at which management said the next phase would be set out and that 'we don't believe that EUR 500 million is the ceiling', moved the shares to EUR 4.20 on 147,766 units and was fully given back the following session at EUR 3.88. When the plan presentation round-trips in a day, the operating story is not what is holding the price.

The honest summary: the only event that re-rates this security is a decision by JD.com to pay for the rest of the company, and JD has no obligation to make it, no announced intention to make it, and a direct economic interest in the share price staying low until it does.
valley_of_death:
There is no cash-burn hump and no maturity wall here. The risks over the next three to nine months are the ordinary kind, plus one structural trap that is specific to this security.

Solvency is not the concern. At 30 June 2026 the company held EUR 1,091 million of cash against EUR 2,597 million of total debt, of which roughly EUR 1.7 billion is capitalised store rent rather than borrowing; on a pre-lease basis it sits close to net cash. Suppliers finance the working capital, with a cash conversion cycle of negative 34 days, and capital spending is trivial at about EUR 33 million a quarter against EUR 168 million of depreciation. The financial-strength score of 2.3 on the standard bankruptcy screen looks alarming and is a false reading for a negative-working-capital retailer.

What can go wrong, in order of likelihood.

The first is the seasonal cash swing, which is violent and will be misread. Net debt was nil at 31 December 2025, EUR 1,596 million at 31 March 2026 and EUR 1,506 million at 30 June 2026. The March quarter alone showed a EUR 1,483 million cash outflow as the Christmas payables unwound. Anyone marking this position on a quarterly balance sheet without adjusting for the cycle will see leverage appearing and disappearing that is not real.

The second is the fiscal year ending 30 September 2026, which is the moment the three-year plan comes due. Management set a EUR 500 million adjusted operating profit target at the 2023 capital-markets day and has repeated it 'precisely to the last decimal since'. Nine of nine key indicators fall due on that date. Two things could disappoint. The German and Austrian markets have been described as soft on both the February and May calls, with the region starting the year 'slightly below expectation from an EBIT perspective, mainly driven by top line', and Germany is roughly a third of the business. And the target is measured on the adjusted figure; the reported figure has run about EUR 300 million lower every year for three years, so hitting the target and reporting another near-zero net profit are entirely compatible outcomes.

The third is the regulatory tail on the JD transaction, which the current market regime says to take more seriously than usual. As of 13 May 2026 foreign-investment approvals were still outstanding in Austria, Germany and Spain, and the European foreign-subsidies review in Brussels was described only as constructive discussions. The regime read of 18 August 2026 is explicit that clearance-based deal-risk models are now mis-specified: Paramount's transaction satisfied every regulatory condition and cleared 68 countries and is frozen regardless, to a 2027 trial. A Chinese buyer of European retail infrastructure and customer data faces exactly the kind of political review that does not resolve on a schedule. The 10 November 2026 long-stop date falls inside the nine-month window.

The fourth, and the one that has no natural end, is that nothing happens. There is no dividend. The shares have de-rated from EUR 4.49 on 20 March 2026 to EUR 3.975, drifting down through a summer in which the operating results improved. A holder waiting for a controlling shareholder to decide receives nothing for waiting.

The fifth is liquidity itself. On 31 August 2026 the shares traded 6,252 units, roughly EUR 25,000 for a session. In an adverse tape, this is a security in which the exit is priced, not offered.
positioning_washout:
The forced selling has already happened, which is precisely why there is no washout left to buy.

The shareholder base was reshaped in one move. JD.com's tender took it to 85.2% by the end of November 2025, and every institution that wanted the offer price took it. What remains is a 14.8% float of roughly 72 million shares, worth about EUR 285 million. On 31 August 2026 that float turned over 6,252 shares.

The shares traded EUR 4.49 on 20 March and EUR 4.26 on 30 March on 436,130 shares, the heaviest session in the six months of data reviewed, and never recovered the level. We do not have a source naming the cause and will not assert one, but the flow is real and it is behind us, not ahead of us.

That is small, but in a stub with no float it is a real overhang.

# CECONOMY AG (CEC.DE) — Forensic Interrogator Dossier
**Date of review:** 31 August 2026 · **Price used:** EUR 3.975 (XETRA close, 31 Aug 2026) · **Market value:** about EUR 1.93 billion
**Transcripts reviewed:** 17 December 2025 (full-year 2024/25), 11 February 2026 (first quarter 2025/26), 13 May 2026 (second quarter and half year 2025/26)

CECONOMY is the German holding company behind MediaMarkt and Saturn, the largest consumer-electronics retail chain in Europe, with roughly 1,000 stores across 11 countries and about EUR 24 billion of annual sales. Since November 2025 it has been 85.2%-owned by JD.com, the Chinese e-commerce group, following a takeover offer whose acceptance window has closed.

---

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC

Across these three calls the story does not change — and that consistency is the single most striking feature of the file. Management tells the same story in the same words three times, with the numbers moving in the promised direction each time.

The spine of it is a claimed shift "from a classical retailer into what we call an omnichannel service platform" (December 2025), repeated almost verbatim in February and May. The proof points are always the same four: consecutive quarters of profitability growth (11 in December, 12 in February), a rising Net Promoter Score (a customer-recommendation gauge: 61, then 61, then 62), a rising online share of sales (30% at its peak in the first quarter), and a rising contribution from what management calls "growth businesses" — retail media (selling advertising space to suppliers), services and solutions, a third-party marketplace, private label, and renting out floor space.

What genuinely expands over the three calls is that last item, and it expands with numbers rather than adjectives. Growth businesses went from 31% of gross profit in fiscal 2022/23 to 33%, then 36% (December 2025), then "approximately 40% of our gross profit, up from 35% a year ago" (May 2026). By February this was "already a EUR 1 billion business" on a full-year basis. That is the one part of the narrative that is doing real work.

What quietly contracts is Germany. In December the domestic market is barely discussed. By February it is "softer demand in Germany and Austria." By May it is "demand in Germany and Austria remains somewhat subdued, but we are managing that actively," with an admission that the region "started Q1 slightly below expectation from an EBIT perspective, mainly driven by top line." The remedy offered is narrower each time — by May it has shrunk to "extreme focus on the top 200" products, which management says are 40% of sales. A retailer that has retreated to defending 200 stock-keeping units out of 15,000 online is not describing a strong home market.

What is introduced and never developed is JD.com. Every call carries a JD section; none of them contains a number, a synergy target, or a named initiative. In December it is "significant experience, especially in logistics and technology." In February, asked directly whether the Joybuy Express delivery service is coming to MediaMarkt, the chief executive answers "it is too early to comment on specific services." In May the question is only about approval timing. Three calls, three deflections. Whatever value JD brings, management has not quantified one euro of it in public.

Finally, the leadership changed mid-story. Kai-Ulrich Deissner opened the May call by noting it was "my 14th, but also my last earnings call" and introduced the chief financial officer, Remko Rijnders, as "my soon-to-be successor." A chief-financial-officer-to-chief-executive handover, executed while a controlling shareholder waits on regulatory clearance, is a continuity choice, not a change of direction.

---

## 2. CLAIMS vs FINANCIALS (forensic)

This is where the file breaks in two. The operating claims hold up well. The claims a shareholder actually gets paid on do not.

Nine-month reported operating profit is about EUR 161 million and nine-month net income swung to positive EUR 23 million from negative EUR 4 million a year earlier. | Holds — on the adjusted measure |
| Sales growing | All three calls | The June-2026 quarter delivered EUR 5,273 million against EUR 4,803 million a year earlier, up 9.8% — the fastest growth in the series. Nine-month sales EUR 18,345 million, up 4.1%. | Holds, and better than guided |

Reported net income was negative EUR 39 million in 2023, positive EUR 76 million in 2024, negative EUR 35 million in 2025. Trailing-twelve-month diluted earnings per share is negative EUR 0.03. Return on invested capital is 1.8%. Five straight years in which the company earned essentially nothing for its owners. | **Diverges** |

What is causing the EBIT to be negative is the investment that we did in our future" | Dec 2025 | This is the central forensic issue. In 2024/25, adjusted operating profit of EUR 378 million sat on top of a *negative* reported operating result.
